PHENOMENOLOGY OF MIND
429
VOL. II.—B

## (B B)

# SPIRIT *

[In the preceding section, the attempt of individuality to act as its own legislator and judge of laws applying to individuals is analyzed. Individuality may claim the privilege of stating laws that are universal in character but have their source and inspiration solely in the single individual. Such laws can at best only be regulative and cannot be constitutive of the substance of individuality; for the substance of individuality necessarily involves other individuals within it. In short, individuality is realized only as part of a concrete whole of individuals: its life is drawn from a common life in and with others. To attempt to state laws from itself, as if it could create the conditions of its own inherent universality, can only result in one thing: laws are provided without the content that gives them meaning, or else the laws and the content remain entirely external to one another. But if laws are purely formal, they cease to be "laws"—that is, the constitutive conditions of individuality. Hence, the attempt described above is certain to fail due to its own futility. To give the laws meaning, the concrete substance of social life is required; and when this concrete substance is provided, the attempt of individuality to create laws disappears *ipso facto*, for these laws are already found operating in social life. Only such laws have reality. But this involves the further step that individuality is realized—and finds its true universal content—only in and with the order of a society. Here alone is individuality what it is in truth: simultaneously a particular focus of self-consciousness and a realization of universal mind. This condition, where individuality is conscious of itself only in and with others, and conscious of the common life as its own, is the stage of spiritual existence. Spiritual existence and social life thus go together. The following section begins the analysis of this phase of experience, which extends from the simplest form of sociality—the Family—up to the highest experience of universal mind—Religion.

The immediately succeeding section may be taken as the keystone of the entire arch of experience traversed in the *Phenomenology*. Here it is pointed out that all the preceding phases of experience have not merely been preparing the way for what follows, but that the various aspects, previously treated as separate moments of experience, are in reality abstractions from the life of concrete spirit now to be discussed and analyzed.

It is noteworthy that from this point onward, the argument is less negative in its result—either directly or indirectly—and is more systematic and constructive. This is no doubt largely because, up to this point, individual mind as such has been under review, and this is an abstraction from social mind or spiritual existence.]

---

<note>* The term "Spirit" seems to render the word "Geist" used here better than the word "mind" would. Up to this stage of experience, the word "mind" is sufficient to convey the meaning. But spirit is mind at a much higher level of existence.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the transition from individualistic law-making to "Spirit," where true individuality is found through participation in social life and the collective order. It marks a shift in the text toward a more constructive analysis of how individual consciousness integrates into the universal mind of society.</summary>
<keywords>Spirit, Geist, phenomenology, individuality, universality, social life, universal mind, spiritual existence, sociality, religion, ipso facto</keywords>

# VI

## SPIRIT

REASON is spirit when its certainty of being all reality has been raised to the level of truth, and reason is consciously aware of itself as its own world, and of the world as itself. The development of spirit was indicated in the immediately preceding movement of mind, where the object of consciousness—the category pure and simple—rose to be the notion of reason. When reason “observes,” this pure unity of the ego and existence, the unity of subjectivity and objectivity, of being-for-itself and being-in-itself—this unity is immanent; it has the character of implicitness or of being, and the consciousness of reason *finds itself*. But the true nature of “observation” is rather the transcendence of this instinct of *finding* its object lying directly at hand and passing beyond this unconscious state of existence. The directly perceived (*angeschaut*) <note>“Angeschaut” refers to something apprehended through intuition or direct perception.</note> category, the thing simply “found,” enters consciousness as the self-existence of the ego—the ego, which now knows itself in objective reality and knows itself there as the *self*. But this feature of the category—namely, of being for-itself as opposed to being immanent within itself—is equally one-sided, and is a moment that cancels itself. The category, therefore, takes on for consciousness the character which it possesses in its universal truth—it is self-contained

<summary>This page defines Spirit as Reason that has become conscious of itself as the entirety of reality, moving beyond the mere "observation" of objects to recognize itself within objective existence. It explains that the "category" of reason must transcend its status as something simply found or perceived to become a self-contained, universal truth.</summary>
<keywords>Reason, Spirit, Consciousness, Ego, Category, Subjectivity, Objectivity, Immanence, Self-existence, Hegel, Phenomenology of Mind</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the discussion of Reason as a self-contained category to the definition of Spirit as the ethical substance that has become conscious of itself through the interaction of individuals within their world.</meta>

essential reality (an und fürsichseyndes Wesen). This character, still abstract, which constitutes the nature of absolute fact, of “fact itself,” is to begin with “spiritual reality” (das geistige Wesen); and its mode of consciousness here is a formal <insert>knowledge</insert> of that reality, a knowledge which is occupied with its varied and manifold content. This consciousness is still, in point of fact, a particular individual distinct from the general substance, and either prescribes arbitrary laws or pretends to possess within its own knowledge as such the laws as they absolutely are (an und für sich), and takes itself to be the power that passes judgment on them. Or again, looked at from the side of the substance, this is seen to be the self-contained and self-sufficient spiritual reality, which is not yet a consciousness of its own self. The self-contained and self-sufficient reality, however, which is at once aware of being actual in the form of consciousness and presents itself to itself, is Spirit.

Its essential spiritual being (Wesen) has been designated above as the ethical substance; spirit, however, is concrete ethical actuality (Wirklichkeit). Spirit is the *self* of the actual consciousness, to which spirit stands opposed, or rather which appears over against itself as an objective actual world that has lost, however, all sense of strangeness for the self, just as the self has lost all sense of having a dependent or independent existence by itself, cut off and separated from that world. Being substance and universal self-identical permanent essence (Wesen), spirit is the immovable irreducible basis and the starting point for the action of each and every one; it is their purpose and their goal, because it is the ideally implicit nature (Ansich) of all self-conscious-

<summary>This page defines Spirit as the realized ethical substance where consciousness no longer views the objective world as foreign, but as its own self. Spirit is described as the foundational reality and the ultimate goal that unites individual action with universal essence.</summary>
<keywords>Spirit, Hegel, ethical substance, Wesen, Wirklichkeit, Ansich, consciousness, spiritual reality, absolute fact, self-identity</keywords>

# *Phenomenology of Mind*

Taken in isolation, they appear as if they existed on their own. The living ethical world is spirit in its truth. This self-consciousness, taking now the form of Morality (the inner moral life), understands itself as the essential truth, and understands the real essence as its actual self. It no longer places its world, foundation, and basis outside of itself, but lets everything fade into itself; in the form of Conscience (*Gewissen*), spirit is sure and certain (*gewiss*) of itself.

## OBJECTIVE SPIRIT,*—THE ETHICAL ORDER†

Spirit, in its ultimate simple truth, is consciousness, and it breaks its moments apart from one another. An act divides spirit into spiritual substance on one side and consciousness of that substance on the other; it divides the substance as well as the consciousness. The substance appears in the form of a universal inner nature and purpose, standing in contrast to itself *as* particularized reality. The middle or mediating term, infinite in character, is self-consciousness. Being *implicitly* the unity of itself and that substance, it now becomes so explicitly (*for itself/für sich*); it unites the universal inner nature and its particular realization, raises the latter to the former, and becomes ethical action. On the other hand, it brings the former down to the latter and carries out the purpose—the substance presented merely in thought. In this way, it brings to light the unity of itself and the substance, and produces this unity in the form of a "work" performed, and thus as an actual concrete fact (*Wirklichkeit*).

When consciousness breaks up into these elements, the simple substance has partly preserved the attitude of opposition to self-consciousness; partly, it thereby manifests in itself the very nature of consciousness, which consists in distinguishing its own content within

# THE ETHICAL WORLD: LAW HUMAN AND DIVINE: MAN AND WOMAN

[The first step in the analysis of spirit is to take spirit as a realized, actual social order, immediately given as a historical fact and present directly to the minds of the individuals who compose it. It is spirit as an objectively embodied whole of essentially spiritual individuals, without any consciousness of opposition to one another or to the whole, and with an absolute, unbroken sense of their own security and fulfillment within the substance of the social mind. But such a self-complete type of experience has various levels of realization. It cannot exist except through the union of opposing elements; and the central principle of all experience—self-consciousness, which takes such a concrete form here—has abundant material on which to exercise its function of creating and uniting distinctions. The first level is determined by the fact that the substance of social life is made up of the quasi-natural phenomena of human genus and species, of race and nationality, on one hand, and the purely natural element of specialized individual sex on the other. These two aspects go together; the sex relations of individuals maintain race and nationality, and the nation lives in and through its sexually distinct individuals. The social order, as an order, is realized and maintained through these elements. The fact that this order is an order of universal mind gives it a permanence, an inviolability, and an absoluteness that are inseparable from it—so inseparable that the order is viewed as having its roots in the Absolute Mind and as deriving its authority from it. From this perspective, the social order consists of a divinely established and divinely sanctioned regime; the gods are the guardians of the city, the hearth, and the home. On the other hand, the expression of this order varies and is stated from time to time throughout the history of a community. The order in this sense is made by man; the law of the social order thus becomes a human law, determined by human conditions and human ends; it is a cycle of conventions and customs. These two forms of order are inseparable in the life of a community, and they exist together and side

## THE ETHICAL WORLD: HUMAN AND DIVINE LAW: MAN AND WOMAN

The simple substance of spirit, which is consciousness, divides itself into parts. In other words, just as the consciousness of abstract sensory existence transitions into perception, so does the immediate certainty of real ethical existence. And just as for sensory perception bare "being" becomes a "thing" with many properties, so for ethical perception a given act becomes a reality involving many ethical relations. For the former, once again, the unnecessary plurality of properties concentrates into the form of an essential opposition between the individual and the universal. Even more so for the latter—which is consciousness purified and substantial—the plurality of ethical moments is reduced to and assumes a twofold form: that of a law of individuality and a law of universality. Each of these areas or "masses" of the substance remains, however, spirit in its entirety. If in sensory perception "things" have no other substantial reality than the two determinations of the individual and the universal, these determinations express, in the present instance, merely the superficial opposition of both sides to one another.

Individuality, in the case of the subject (*Wesen* <note>the inner essence or being</note>) we are considering here, has the significance of self-consciousness in general, not of any particular consciousness we might choose. The ethical substance is, therefore, in this

# The Ethical World

determined, actual, concrete substance—Absolute Spirit realized in the multitude of distinct and existing consciousnesses. It [this spirit] is the community (*Gemeinwesen*) which appeared to us as the absolute and ultimate reality when we entered the stage where reason is practically embodied. Here, it appears objectively to itself in its true nature as a conscious ethical reality (*Wesen*) and as the essential reality for the mode of consciousness we are currently examining. It is spirit that exists *for itself*, because it maintains itself by being reflected in the minds of the individuals who compose it; and it exists *in itself*, or as substance, because it preserves those individuals within itself. As an actual substance, that spirit is a Nation (*Volk*); as a concrete consciousness, it consists of the Citizens of a nation. This consciousness finds its essential being in simple spirit and is certain of itself through the actual realization of this spirit within the entire nation. It finds its truth there directly—not in something unreal, but in a spirit that exists and makes itself felt.

This spirit can be called Human Law, because its being essentially takes the form of self-conscious actuality. In its universal form, that spirit is law known to everyone, familiar and recognized, and exists as everyday Customary Convention (*Sitte*). In its particular form, it is the concrete certainty that every individual has of themselves; and the certainty of itself as a single individuality is that spirit in the form of Government. Its true and complete nature is seen in its authoritative validity, which is openly and unmistakably manifested as an existence taking the form of unconstrained, independent, and objective fact.

Although the ethical existence of the family has the character of immediacy, it is an *ethical* entity within itself. Let us see what its peculiar ethical character consists of.

In the first place, because the ethical element is the inherently universal element, the ethical relationship between the members of the family is not one of sentiment or the relationship of love. In this case, the ethical element seems bound to be placed in the relationship of the individual member of the family to the entire family as the real substance. In this way, the purpose of his action and the content of his reality are taken from this substance and are derived solely from the family life. stronger than himself—the former because of the life they possess, the latter because of their negative nature. <note>The description here refers to the process of bodily corruption.</note> The family protects the dead from this dishonoring by the desires of unconscious organic agencies and by abstract elements; it puts its own action in place of theirs and marries the relative to the bosom of the earth, the elemental individuality that does not pass away. Through this, the family makes the deceased a member of a community <note>That is, the earth?</note> that prevails over and holds under control the powers of the particular material elements and the lower living creatures, which sought to have their way with the dead and destroy him.

This final duty thus fulfills the complete divine law, or constitutes the positive ethical act toward the specific individual. Every other relationship toward him that does not remain at the level of love, but is ethical, belongs to human law; it has the negative significance of lifting the individual above the confinement within the natural community to which he belongs as a concrete individual. But now, although human right draws its content and power from the actual ethical substance consciously aware of itself—the entire nation—while divine right and law derive theirs from the particular individual who is beyond the actual world, that individual is still not without power. His power lies in the abstract pure universal, the shadowy individual, which seizes upon the individuality that cuts itself loose from the element and constitutes the self-conscious reality of the nation, and draws it back into the pure abstraction which is the essential nature of the shadowy individual, while at the same time the latter is its ultimate foundation.

Now, in both the one law and the other, there are differences and stages. Since these laws involve the element of consciousness in both cases, distinctions develop within them; and this is exactly what constitutes the specific process of their life. Examining these differences reveals how they operate and the kind of self-consciousness at work in both the universal essential principles (*Wesen*) of the ethical world, as well as their connection and transition into one another.

The community—the higher law whose validity is open to the light of day—makes its concrete activity felt in government; for in government, it acts as an individual whole. Government is concrete, actual Spirit reflected into itself—the pure and simple self of the entire ethical substance. This simple force allows the community to unfold and expand into its component members, and to give each part its own subsistence and self-existence (*Fürsichseyn*). In this way, Spirit finds its realization or its objective existence, and the family is the medium through which this realization takes effect. But at the same time, Spirit is the force of the whole, reuniting these parts within the unity that negates their independence. It gives them a sense of their lack of self-sufficiency and keeps them aware that their life exists only within the whole. Thus, on one hand, the community may organize itself into systems of property and personal independence, of personal rights and rights over things; on the other hand, it can articulate the various ways of working for what, in the first instance, are particular interests.

By breaking up the form of fixed stability in this way, spirit prevents the ethical order from sinking into a merely natural existence, preserves the self of which it is conscious, and raises that self to the level of freedom and its own powers. This essential negative being proves to be the true power of the community and the force it uses for self-preservation. Therefore, the community finds the true principle and confirmation of its power in the inner nature of divine law and in the kingdom of the underworld.

The relationship between husband and wife is initially the primary and immediate way in which one consciousness recognizes itself in another, and in which each finds mutual recognition. As a form of natural self-knowledge—knowledge of the self based on nature rather than on ethical life—it only represents and symbolizes the life of spirit through a figure; it is not spirit itself in its fully realized form. However, this symbolic representation is realized in something other than itself. Therefore, this relationship is not realized within itself as such, but in the child—an "other" whose very birth constitutes the relationship and through whom that relationship passes away. This transition from one generation to the next is a permanent feature in the life of a nation.

The reverent devotion (*Pietät*) of husband and wife for one another is thus mixed with a natural relationship and with feeling, and their relationship is not complete in itself; the same applies to the second relationship: the reverent devotion between parents and children. Parental devotion is affected and disrupted because it is consciously realized in something external to the parents (the children), and by seeing the children become independent individuals without this independence returning to the parents. The children's independent existence remains a separate reality, entirely their own. Conversely, the devotion of children toward their parents is affected by the fact that they originate from, or have their essential nature in, something external to them (the parents) that eventually passes away; they achieve their own independent existence and self-consciousness only through separation.

Both of these relationships are formed by and maintained within the transience and the dissimilarity of the two sides assigned to them.

However, a pure and non-transitional form of relationship exists between brother and sister. They share the same blood, which has achieved a state of stable equilibrium within them. Therefore, they do not stand in a natural relationship like that of husband and wife; they do not desire one another. Nor have they given to or received from each other this independence of individual existence; they are free individuals in relation to one another. Therefore, the feminine element, in the form of the sister, most completely anticipates and foreshadows the nature of ethical life (*sittliches Wesen*). She does not become conscious of it and does not actualize it because the law of the family is her inherent, implicit, inward nature. This nature does not lie open to the daylight of consciousness but remains an inner feeling and a divine element exempt from actual existence. Feminine life is attached to these household divinities (*Penates*) and sees in them both her universal substance and her particular individuality. Yet, she views them in such a way that her specific relationship to them is not the natural one of pleasure.

As a daughter, the woman must now watch her parents pass away with natural emotion and yet with ethical resignation, for it is only through this condition that she can achieve the individual existence of which she is capable. The husband is sent out by the spirit of the family into the life of the community, where he finds his self-conscious reality. Just as the family finds its universal substance and support in the community, the community, in turn, finds in the family the formal element of its own realization, and in the divine law its power and confirmation. Neither of the two is complete on its own. Human law, as a living and active principle, proceeds from the divine—the law of the earth from that of the underworld, the conscious from the unconscious, mediation from immediacy—and it returns to where it began. The power of the underworld, on the other hand, finds its realization on earth; through consciousness, it comes to have existence and effect.

The whole is a stable equilibrium of all its parts, and each part is a spirit in its native element—a spirit that does not seek its satisfaction beyond itself, but finds satisfaction within itself because it exists in this balanced state with the whole. This condition of stable equilibrium can, of course, only remain vital if inequality arises within it and is brought back to balance by Righteousness and Justice. Justice, however, is neither an alien principle (*Wesen*) existing somewhere remote from the present, nor is it the realization (unworthy of the name of justice) of mutual malice, treachery, ingratitude, and so on, which would fulfill the law through the unintelligent path of chance and accident—an irrational connection lacking any controlling idea, consisting of actions and omissions performed without any awareness of what was involved. On the contrary, as justice within human law, it restores to the whole—to the universal life of society—whatever has broken away from the harmony and equilibrium of the whole: namely, the independent classes and individuals. In this way, justice is the government of the nation; it is its all-pervading, essential life in a consciously present individual form, and it is the personal, self-conscious will of all.

Of these movements, the former belongs to man, and the latter to woman.

### ETHICAL ACTION. KNOWLEDGE, HUMAN AND DIVINE. GUILT AND DESTINY.

A fundamental condition of social order is that it is maintained by the actions of the individual members of a society. Action is the fundamental principle that distinguishes individuals; it is the way they contribute to social life and also the means through which the continuity of social life is constantly broken and rebuilt. In a broad sense, therefore, action is the principle by which distinction within unity is realized in social life. Examining its significance is thus an essential problem for the analysis of the "social mind." Action must be considered both in relation to individuality and in relation to those concepts of social order that contain both "divine" and "human" law. In the following section, this analysis is undertaken.

The specific historical background for Hegel’s thought in this section, and to some extent in the preceding section, is provided by the social life of the Greek city-state. The Greek city-state is taken as the model, so to speak, of a spiritual existence realized as a self-contained ethical order. However, Greek social life is largely interpreted here through the dramatization of Greek ethical concepts by the great Greek tragedians, especially Sophocles. This explains the repeated references to the purely dramatic concept of "destiny" or the <term>pathic</term> element <note>The "pathic" element refers to the aspect of being acted upon or experiencing fate, as opposed to being the active agent.</note> in the life of an individual whose spiritual existence is entirely tied to the established social order. It is in Greece that we find the most complete realization of the state's total self-sufficiency for the individual, which is Hegel's focus here—a sufficiency that was simultaneously the strength and beauty, as well as the pathos and weakness, of Greek social life.

With this and the preceding section, one should read Hegel’s *Philosophy of History*, Part II, “The Greek World.”

<summary>This introduction explains that ethical action is the means by which individuals maintain and transform social order, balancing personal identity with universal law. It notes that Hegel bases his analysis on the Greek city-state, specifically as interpreted through the tragedies of Sophocles and the tension between destiny and the state.</summary>

In the form presented by the conflict of elements in the realm just discussed, self-consciousness has not yet achieved its rights as a specific individual identity. In that realm, individuality is understood, on one hand, as a purely universal will, and on the other, as the kinship of the family. This specific individual has only the significance of a shadowy unreality. As of yet, no action has been performed. The act, however, is the realized self. It disrupts the undisturbed, stable organization and movement of the ethical world. What appears there as an established order and harmony between its two constituent elements—each of which validates and completes the other—becomes, through the performance of an act, a transition of opposites into one another. Through this transition, each element proves to be the destruction rather than the validation of itself and its opposite. It becomes a process of negation or destruction—the eternal necessity of a terrifying destiny that swallows both divine and human law into the abyss of its simple identity, as well as both self-conscious factors in which these powers reside. From our perspective, this process passes into the absolute self-existence of a purely individual self-consciousness.

The foundation from which this movement begins, and upon which it operates, is the realm of the ethical order. However, the activity driving this process is self-consciousness. As an ethical consciousness, it is the

<meta>This page continues the discussion on ethical consciousness, exploring its direct relationship to duty and how it avoids internal conflict by identifying with either divine or human law based on natural assignment.</meta>

pure and simple direction of activity towards the essential principle of the ethical life—it is *Duty*. There is no caprice, and likewise no struggle or indecision in it, since it has given up legislating and testing laws: for this consciousness, the essential ethical principle is something immediate, unwavering, and without contradiction. There is, therefore, neither the painful spectacle of finding itself in a conflict between passion and duty, nor the comic spectacle of a conflict between duty and duty—a conflict which, as far as its content goes, is the same as that between passion and duty. For passion can also be presented as a duty, because duty—when consciousness withdraws into itself and leaves its immediate essential substance (*Wesenheit*)—becomes a formal universal into which one content fits just as well as another, as we found before. The conflict of duties is, however, comical because it brings out the contradiction inherent in the idea of one absolute standing opposed to another absolute; it expresses something as absolute and then immediately expresses the annihilation of this so-called absolute or duty. The ethical consciousness, however, knows what it has to do; and it is decided whether it is to belong to divine or human law. This directness which characterizes its decision is something immanent and inherent (*Ansichseyn*), and hence has at the same time the significance of a natural condition of being, as we saw. Nature, not the accident of circumstances or choice, assigns one sex to one law and the other sex to the other law; or, conversely, both ethical powers themselves establish their individual existence and actualization in the two sexes.

<header>Ethical Action</header>

The absolute right of ethical self-consciousness comes into conflict with the divine right of the essential reality. Self-consciousness, *as* consciousness, takes objective reality, as such, to have essential being. However, when looking at its substance, it is the unity of itself and this opposite, and ethical self-consciousness is the consciousness of that substance. Therefore, the object—as something opposed to self-consciousness—has entirely lost the characteristic of having essential being on its own. Just as the stages [of conscious life] where the object is merely a "thing" are long gone, so too are those stages where consciousness establishes something from within itself and turns a particular moment into the essential reality (*Wesen*). Against such one-sidedness, actual concrete reality has a power of its own; it takes the side of truth against consciousness and shows consciousness itself what the truth is. The ethical consciousness, however, has drunk from the cup of the absolute substance and forgotten all the one-sidedness of isolated self-existence, along with all its own purposes and peculiar notions. Therefore, it has at the same time drowned in this Stygian stream all the inherent essence of nature and all the independence claimed by objective reality. Its absolute right, therefore, when it acts in accordance with ethical law, is to find in this realization nothing other than the fulfillment and performance of this law itself: and that the deed should manifest nothing but ethical action.

The ethical, being absolute essence and absolute power at once, cannot endure any perversion of its content. If it were merely absolute essence without power, it might undergo perversion at the hands of

Through the act, it thus becomes *Guilt*. For the deed is its own doing, and doing is its inmost nature. This guilt also acquires the meaning of *Crime*; for as a simple ethical consciousness, it has turned toward and conformed itself to one law but has turned away from the other, thereby breaking the latter by its deed.

Guilt is not an external, indifferent entity (*essential nature*) with a double meaning—as if the deed, as it is actually manifested in the light of day, might be an action of the guilty self or might not be. It is not as if something external and accidental, which did not belong to the deed, could be connected to it—a point of view from which the action would therefore be innocent. Rather, the act is itself this diremption, this affirming of itself for itself, and the establishing of an alien, external reality over against it. That such a result occurs is due to the deed itself and is its outcome. Hence, innocence is an attribute merely of the lack of action (*non-action*), a state like the mere existence of a stone, and one which is not even true of a child.

Looking at the content, however, the ethical act contains the element of wrongdoing because it does not cancel or transcend the natural allotment of the two laws to the two sexes. Instead, by maintaining an undivided attitude toward the law, it stays within the sphere of natural immediacy; as it acts (*qua* acting), it turns this one-sidedness into guilt by merely seizing one side of the essential reality and taking up a negative relationship toward the other—that is, violating it. ## THE CONDITION OF RIGHT OR LEGAL STATUS

[A further step in realizing the principle of coherent sociality is reached when the individual is granted the universality of the social order through specific laws enacted by the governing power of the social whole. His status as a random individual is removed because he is explicitly treated as a central unity of the entire order. The very existence of that order depends on maintaining him as a unit with universal significance, and the system stands or falls by keeping him in this condition. In this case, the universal order is no longer merely implicit or a matter of routine and custom; it is openly and objectively expressed in and through every individual member of society. This takes the form of dividing the social substance into a collection of “persons,” all of whom are granted explicit universal or legally acknowledged significance. This is the realm of legal personality, or of individuality established by a system of Rights. It is a supreme achievement of social life and the highest point of coherent social experience. This is the focus of the current section.

This condition or stage exists in every developed community. However, the specific historical material for this section is drawn from the legally constituted social order of the Roman Empire, particularly the Empire under the Antonines. Here, whether by coincidence or otherwise, the peak of imperial rule and the “golden age” of law occurred simultaneously. The triumph of the Roman imperial government and the perfection of the system of Roman jurisprudence were achieved during the same period, roughly from <term>A.D.</term> 131–235. There is every reason to believe that the two necessarily rose and fell together, and that the decline and disappearance of the Roman legal state prepared the way for a further achievement of the social spirit of humanity. This provides the historical justification for the transition to the next stage of social life: that of a self-conflicted spiritual existence.

With this section, one should read Hegel’s *Philosophy of History*, Part III, especially the introduction to that part and Section III, chapter 1, “Rome under the Emperors.”]

## THE CONDITION OF RIGHT OR LEGAL STATUS

The general, comprehensive unity into which the living, immediate unity of individuality and the ethical substance collapses is the soulless (*geistlos*) community. It has ceased to be the unconscious <note>Reading “*selbstbewusstlose*” (1st ed.).</note> substance of individuals, and in this community, they now—each in their separate individual existence—count as selves and substances with an existence of their own. With the universal being thus split into the atomic units of a mere plurality of individuals, this inactive, lifeless spirit becomes a principle of equality where everyone counts as much as anyone else—that is, they have the significance of *Persons*. What was called the hidden divine law in the realm of ethical life has, in fact, emerged from concealment into the light of reality. In the former state, the individual was—and was considered—real merely as a blood relative, or merely as a participant in the general life of the family. As a particular individual, he was the selfless, departed spirit; now, however, he has emerged from his unreality. Because the ethical substance is only objective, “true” spirit—only implying spirit—the individual consequently turns back to the immediate certainty of his own self. He is that substance as a positive universal, but his reality consists in being a negative universal self.

Consciousness of right, therefore, in the course of the very process of making its claim good, finds that it loses its own reality, discovers its complete lack of inherent substantiality, and finds that to describe an individual as a “person” is to use an expression of contempt.

## B

# SPIRIT IN SELF-ESTRANGEMENT—THE DISCIPLINE OF CULTURE

[The life of spirit, as found in social self-consciousness, has two fundamental factors: the universal spirit (or social whole as such) and the individual member as such. The interaction between these two constitutes the spiritual existence of society. Each factor by itself is abstract; however, the realization of a complete spiritual life through and within each is absolutely essential for spiritual fulfillment. In the previous analysis of spirit, one form of this process was considered: the realization of the objective social order in and through individuals. In the following section and its various subsections, the other process for achieving the same general result is analyzed: the movement where, starting from the individual spirit, the realization of complete spiritual existence is established. The first process starts from the compact solidarity of the social substance and results in the establishment of separate and individually complete legal personalities. The second process starts from the rigidly exclusive unity of the individual self and results in the establishment of a social order made of absolutely universal and, therefore, absolutely free wills. Both processes are *per se* abstract, despite being necessary; therefore, as we shall find, a further stage in the evolution of spirit must still appear.]

The process of spirit in this second stage assumes from the start a conscious contrast between the individual spirit and a universal spiritual whole—a contrast that, while profound, the individual seeks to remove because the universality of spiritual existence he aims to achieve is implicitly involved in his very being as a spiritual entity. To begin with, his spiritual life seems torn in two, so complete is the sense of opposition between the factors that constitute his life. His true life—his objective embodiment—seems to be entirely outside him, yet he feels it to be his own self. He seems “estranged” from his complete self, and this estrangement seems to be of his own making, because the substance from which he is cut off is felt to be his own. This contrast is the deepest that spirit can possibly experience, simply because spirit is and knows itself to be self-contained and self-complete—“the only reality.” The contrast can only be removed through effort and struggle, for the individual spirit must create or recreate for itself, and by its own activity, a universal objective spiritual realm, which

<summary>This page introduces the second stage of spirit, where individuals feel estranged from the universal social whole and must work to reconcile their individual selves with a broader spiritual reality. It outlines the transition from a society of legal personalities toward a social order defined by universal and free wills.</summary>

<keywords>Spirit, Self-estrangement, Culture, Social self-consciousness, Universal spirit, Social whole, Spiritual existence, Social substance, Legal personalities, Free wills, Reality</keywords>

it implies, and in which alone it can be free and feel itself at home. The struggle spirit undergoes is thus the greatest in the whole range of its experience, for the opposition to be overcome is the most profound that exists. Since its aim is to achieve the highest for itself, nothing sacred can be allowed to stand in its way. It will make any sacrifice and, if necessary, produce the direst spiritual disaster—a spiritual “reign of terror”—to accomplish its result.

The movement of spirit analyzed here covers every form of the individual’s “struggle for a substantial spiritual life.” It embraces the “intellectual,” “economic,” “religious,” and “ethical” in the narrower sense of these terms; it embraces all that we mean by “culture” and “civilization.” Hence the various parts of the argument: spiritual “discipline,” “enlightenment,” the pursuit of “wealth,” “belief” and “superstition,” and “absolute freedom.”

The process of spiritual life under critical review here is familiar to a greater or lesser extent in every age and every society. But the actual historical material present to the writer's mind is derived from: (1) the period of European history embracing the entrance of Christianity and Christian philosophy into European civilization after the fall of the Roman Empire, and the intellectual, “humanistic” awakening of the Renaissance which led to the ecclesiastical revolution known as the Reformation; and (2) the rationalistic movement of the eighteenth century, the so-called “Enlightenment,” which preceded and culminated in the French Revolution—the supreme outburst of spiritual emancipation known in European history. These two periods, far removed as they are in time, have much in common. They embody principles of spiritual development that are fundamentally alike and are therefore freely drawn upon in the analysis, regardless of historicity.

Much of Hegel’s analysis of the first stage of this spiritual movement also directly considers the character of Rameau in Diderot’s dialogue *Le neveu de Rameau* (*Rameau's Nephew*). This remarkable work was written in 1760 but was first brought to the attention of the literary public by Goethe, who translated and published the work in 1805. It thus came into Hegel’s hands while he was writing the *Phenomenology*; this perhaps accounts for the repeated references to it in the argument. The term “self-estranged spirit,” with which he heads this section, occurs in Goethe’s translation. Rameau is an extreme type of such a spirit.

With this section, one should read Hegel’s *Philosophy of History*, Pt. III, § 3, c. 2; Pt. IV, § 2, c. 1, § 3, c. 1, 3: the *History of Philosophy*, Pt. 3, Introduction, and c. 2, “The French Philosophy and the German Enlightenment.”]

The ethical substance preserved and kept opposition contained within its simple conscious life; and this consciousness was in direct unity with its own essential nature. That nature, therefore, has the simple characteristic of something that merely exists for the consciousness which is focused directly upon it, and which considers it its "custom" (*Sitte*). Consciousness does not represent a specific, excluded self, nor does the substance mean to it an existence shut out from itself, with which it would have to establish its identity only by alienating itself, while at the same time having to create that alienation. 

But that mind, whose self is completely isolated and entirely separate, finds its content standing against itself in the form of a reality that is just as impenetrable as itself; here, the world takes on the characteristic of being something external and negative to self-consciousness. Yet this world is a spiritual reality; it is essentially the merging of individuality with being. Its existence is the work of self-consciousness, but it is also a reality immediately present and foreign to it, which has a unique existence of its own and in which self-consciousness does not recognize itself. This reality is the external element and the free content* of the domain of legal right. But this external reality, which the master of the world

It preserves its existence through self-consciousness of its own accord, by relinquishing itself and giving up its essential nature. This is the condition that, amidst the waste and ruin prevailing in the sphere of right, the external force of the elements let loose seems to impose upon self-consciousness. These elements by themselves are sheer ruin and destruction, and they cause their own overthrow. This overthrow, however—this negative nature of theirs—is exactly the *self*; it is their subject, their action, and their process. Such process and activity, through which the substance becomes actual, are again the alienation of personality. For the immediate self—that is, the self without estrangement, which is considered valid just as it is—lacks substantial content and is the plaything of these raging elements. Its substance is thus precisely its relinquishment, and this relinquishment is the substance—that is, the spiritual powers forming themselves into a coherent world and thereby securing their continued existence.

The substance in this way is spirit: the self-conscious unity of the self and its essential nature; but both also understand each other to mean and imply alienation. Spirit is the consciousness of an objective reality that exists independently on its own. Yet, standing against this consciousness is that unity of the self with its essential nature—pure and simple consciousness standing over against actual consciousness. Spirit in this case, therefore, constructs not merely one world, but a twofold world, divided and self-opposed. The world of the ethical spirit is its own proper present; and hence every power it possesses is found in this unity of the present, and, so far as each separates itself from the other, each is still in equilibrium with the whole. Nothing has the significance of a negative of self-consciousness; even the spirit of the deceased is in the lifeblood of his relatives, is present in the self of the family, and the universal power of government is the will, the self of the nation. Here, however, what is present means merely objective actuality, which has its consciousness in the "beyond"; each particular moment, as an essential entity, receives this, and thereby its actuality from another, and so far as it is actual, its essential being is something other than its own actuality. Nothing has a spirit that is self-established and dwelling within it; rather, each is outside itself in what is alien to it. The equilibrium of the whole is not the unity which remains by itself, nor its inwardly secured tranquility, but rests on the alienation of its opposite. The whole is, therefore, like each particular moment, a self-estranged reality. But while the former was the first self—the particular person who holds weight directly—this second self, which returns to itself from its own self-surrender, will be the universal self: the consciousness that grasps the concept. These spiritual worlds, whose every element insists on being a fixed reality and an unspiritual existence, will be dissolved in the light of pure insight. This insight, which is the self grasping itself, completes the stage of culture. It accepts nothing but the self and treats everything as the self; that is, it comprehends everything, removes all objectivity, and converts everything implicit into something explicit—transforming everything that has a "being *in itself*" into what is "*for itself*." 

When turned against belief and faith—as the remote region of inner being lying in the distant beyond—it becomes Enlightenment (*Aufklärung*). This Enlightenment also ends self-estrangement in that realm where the self-alienated spirit turns to seek safety, a realm where it becomes conscious of a peace that is adequate to itself. Enlightenment disrupts the household arrangements that the spirit maintains in the "house of faith" by bringing in the goods and furnishings belonging to the world of the here and now—a world that the spirit cannot refuse to accept as its own property, for its conscious life also belongs to it.

# I

## THE WORLD OF SPIRIT IN SELF-ESTRANGEMENT

The sphere of spirit at this stage breaks up into two regions. One is its real world, its self-estrangement; the other is constructed and established in the ether of pure consciousness and is elevated above the first. This second world, being constructed in opposition and contrast to that estrangement, is for that very reason not free from it; on the contrary, it is only another form of that same estrangement, which consists precisely in having a conscious existence in two types of worlds and embraces both. Therefore, it is not the self-consciousness of Absolute Being in and for itself—not Religion—that is dealt with here: it is Belief, or Faith, insofar as faith is a flight from the actual world and thus is not a self-complete experience (*in and for itself*). Such a flight from the realm of the present is, therefore, directly in its very nature a dual state of mind. Pure consciousness is the sphere into which the spirit rises: but it is not only the element of faith, but of the notion as well. Consequently, both appear on the scene together at the same time, and the latter comes before us only in antithesis to the former.

<summary>At this stage, the spirit splits into a real world of estrangement and a secondary world of pure consciousness or faith. This faith is characterized as an escape from reality rather than a complete religious experience, existing in tension with the concept of the "notion."</summary>

<keywords>spirit, self-estrangement, pure consciousness, Absolute Being, Religion, Belief, Faith, in and for itself, notion, antithesis</keywords>

# CULTURE AND ITS SPHERE OF OBJECTIVE REALITY<note>It will be observed that "culture" embraces all means of self-development—"ideas" as well as material factors such as "wealth."</note>

The spirit of this world is a spiritual essence permeated by a self-consciousness that knows itself to be directly present as a self-existent particular, and has that essence as its objective reality standing against itself. But the existence of this world, as well as the reality of self-consciousness, depends on the process by which self-consciousness divests itself of its personality; by doing so, it creates its world and treats it as something alien and external, which it must now take possession of. But the renunciation of its self-existence is itself the production of objective reality, and in doing so, therefore, self-consciousness *ipso facto* makes itself master of this world.

To put the matter otherwise, self-consciousness is only something definite—it only has real existence—insofar as it alienates itself from itself. By doing so, it puts itself in the position of something universal, and this universality actualizes it, establishes it objectively, and makes it valid. This equality of the self with all other selves is, therefore, not the equality that was found in the case of right; self-consciousness does not here, as it did there, receive immediate recognition and acknowledgment merely because it exists. On the contrary, its claim to exist rests on

As a result of this process, the self-contained conscious mind doubtless finds its reality, pure and simple, and its subsistence within the Power of the State; but it does not find its individuality as such. It finds its inherent and essential being, but not what it is for itself. Rather, it finds there that its action, *as* individual action, is rejected and denied, and subdued into obedience. The individual thus recoils before this power and turns back into himself; it is the reality that suppresses him, and is "the bad." For instead of being identical with him—that with which he is at one—it is something utterly in discordance with individuality. In contrast with this, Wealth and Riches are "the good"; they tend toward general enjoyment, they are there simply to be disposed of, and they ensure for everyone the consciousness of his particular self. Riches means in its very nature universal beneficence: if it refuses any benefit in a given case and does not gratify every need, this is merely an accident which does not detract from its universal and necessary nature of imparting to every individual his share and being a thousand-handed benefactor.

This estrangement, however, takes place in **Language**, in words alone, and here language assumes its peculiar *role*. Both in the sphere of the general social order (*Sittlichkeit*), where language conveys laws and commands, and in the sphere of actual life, where it appears conveying advice, the content of what it expresses is the essential reality, and language is the form of that essential content. Here, however, language takes the form in which, *as* language, its existence is its content, and it possesses authority *as* the spoken word; it is the power of utterance *as* utterance which, in the very act of speaking, performs what must be performed. For it is the existence of a pure self *as* self; in speech, the particular self-existent self-consciousness comes into existence as such, so that its particular individuality is something for others.

The **Ego**, *as* this particular pure ego, does not exist otherwise; in every other mode of expression, it is absorbed in some concrete actuality and appears in a shape from which it can withdraw. It turns reflectively back into itself, away from its act as well as from its physical expression, leaving such an incomplete existence (in which there is always at once too much as well as too little) lying soulless behind. The unity, therefore, appears in the role of a mediating term, which is excluded and distinguished from the separated reality of the two sides; it has, therefore, the actual character of something objective, set apart and distinguished from its aspects, and objective for them—that is, the unity is an existing objective fact.

The spiritual substance comes into existence as such only when it has been able to take as its aspects those self-consciousnesses which recognize this pure self as a reality claiming immediate validity. In doing so, they also immediately know that they are such realities merely through the process of alienation. Through that pure self, the moments of substance gain the transparency of a self-knowing category and become clarified enough to be moments of spirit; through this mediating process, spirit comes to exist in spiritual form. Spirit, in this way, is the mediating term, presupposing those extremes and produced through their existence; but it is also the spiritual whole emerging between them, which divides itself into them and creates each solely by virtue of that contact with the whole which belongs to its very principle. The fact that both extremes are, from the start and in their very nature, transcended and disintegrated brings out their unity; and this is the process which fuses both together, interchanges their characteristic features, and binds them together within each extreme. This mediating process consequently actualizes the principle of each of the two extremes, or makes what each is inherently in itself its controlling and moving spirit.

Both extremes—the state authority and the noble type of consciousness—are disintegrated by this latter process. In state power, the two sides are the abstract universal which is obeyed, and the individual will existing for its own sake, which, however, does not yet belong to the universal itself. In nobility, the two sides are obedience in the surrender of existence (or the inherent maintenance of self-respect and honor) and, on the other hand, a self which exists purely for its own sake.

Viewed *in itself*, state-power reflected back into itself—or becoming spiritual—means nothing else than that it has become a moment of self-conscious life; that is, it exists only by being <term>sublated</term> <note>absorbed or transformed while being preserved</note>. Consequently, it is now the real in the sense of something whose spiritual meaning lies in being sacrificed and squandered; it exists in the sense of wealth. It continues, no doubt, to exist at the same time as a form of reality opposed to wealth, into which it is fundamentally always passing; but it is a reality whose inherent principle is this very process of passing over—due to the service and the reverence rendered to it, through which it arises—into its opposite: the condition of relinquishing its power. Thus, from its own point of view (*<term>Fürsich</term>*), the special and unique self that constitutes its will becomes—through the self-abasement of the nobility—a universal that renounces itself. It becomes a completely isolated individual, a mere accident that is the prey of every stronger will. What remains of its universally acknowledged and incommunicable independence is only the empty name.

While the nobility may adopt the attitude of something that can relate to universal power in a similar way, its true nature lies instead in retaining its own separate existence even while rendering its service. However, in what is properly the renunciation of its personality, its true being lies in actually canceling and tearing apart the universal substance. Its spirit is the attitude of thoroughgoing discordance (inequality):

### Culture and its Sphere of Reality

On one hand, it retains its own will through the honor it receives; on the other hand, it gives up its will. In part, it alienates its inner nature from itself and reaches an extreme state of internal discord; in part, it subdues the universal substance to itself and puts this substance entirely at odds with itself. As a result, it is obvious that its own specific nature—which kept it distinct from the so-called "base" type of mind—disappears, and with it, that base type of mind disappears as well. The base type has achieved its goal: that of subordinating universal power to its own self-centered isolation.

Endowed in this way with universal power, self-consciousness exists in the form of universal beneficence; or, from another point of view, universal power is wealth, which is itself an object for consciousness. For wealth is understood here as the universal brought into subjection; however, through this first act of transcendence, it has not yet absolutely returned into the self. The self does not yet have itself as its own object, but instead perceives the universal essential reality in a state of <term>sublation</term> <note>a state of being transformed or overcome while still being preserved</note>. Since this object has only just come into being, the relationship of consciousness toward it is immediate, and consciousness has not yet expressed its lack of harmony with this object. Here, we see the nobility preserving its own self-centered existence within a universal power that has become non-essential; consequently, it acknowledges the object and feels grateful to its benefactor.

Wealth contains within it from the start the aspect of self-existence (<term>*Fürsichsein*</term>). It is not the selfless universal of state-power, or the unconstrained simplicity of the natural life of spirit; it is state-power maintaining its own position through an effort of will, in opposition to a will that seeks to master it and derive enjoyment from it.

Wealth is characterized as state power that is no longer a selfless universal but is instead a contested object of individual will and enjoyment.</summary>

But since wealth has merely the form of being essential, this one-sided self-centered life—which has no being in itself, and which is rather the <term>sublation</term> <note>the process of overcoming or transforming something while still preserving it</note> of inherent being—is the return of the individual into himself only to find no essential reality in his own enjoyment. It therefore needs to be given animation; and its reflective process of bringing this about consists in it becoming something real in itself as well as for itself, instead of being merely for itself. Wealth, which is the transformed essential reality, has to become the essentially real. In this way, it preserves its own spiritual principle within itself.

It will be sufficient here to describe the content of this process, since we have already explained its form at length. Nobility, then, stands here in relation not to the object in the general sense of something essential; what is alien to it is self-centered existence itself. It finds itself face to face with its own self in a state of alienation, appearing as an objective, solid reality which it must take from the hands of another self-centered being—another equally fixed and solid entity. Its object is self-centered existence, that is, its own being; but by being an object, this is at the same time *ipso facto* an alien reality, which is a self-centered being on its own account and has a will of its own. In other words, the noble sees their self under the power of an alien will, on which they depend for the granting of their own selfhood.

Self-consciousness can detach itself from any particular aspect, and for that reason, even when under an obligation to one of these aspects, it retains the recognition and inherent validity of self-consciousness as an independent reality. Here, however, it finds that, as regards its own ego, its own proper and

The spirit of well-doing that characterizes the action of wealth may, further, be distinguished from that of the conscious life accepting the benefit it confers, and it deserves special consideration.

The spirit animating wealth had an unreal, insubstantial independence; wealth was something to be given up. By communicating what it has, however, it passes into something essential and inherent; since it fulfills its nature in sacrificing itself, it cancels the aspect of particularity—of merely seeking enjoyment for one's own particular self—and, being thus sublated *qua* particular, the type of spirit here is universality or essentially real.

What it imparts, what it gives to others, is self-existence. It does not hand itself over, however, as a natural, selfless object—as the frankly and freely offered condition of unconscious life—but as self-conscious, as a reality keeping hold of itself. It is not like the power of an inorganic element, which is felt by the consciousness receiving its force to be inherently transitory; it is the power over self, a power aware that it is independent and voluntary, and knowing at the same time that what it dispenses becomes the self of someone else.

# Culture and its Sphere of Reality

Wealth thus shares in the condemnation along with its clients; but instead of rebellion, arrogance appears. For in one sense it knows, as well as the self it benefits, that its own existence is a matter of chance; yet it is itself this very chance in whose power personality is placed. In this arrogant mood—which thinks it has secured another person’s nature through a gift, and thereby forced their innermost being into submission—it overlooks the other self’s secret rebellion. It overlooks the fact that all bonds have been completely cast aside; it overlooks this pure disintegration. In this state, the self-identity of that which exists for its own sake has become pure internal discord; all unity, harmony, and stability are torn apart, and as a result, the thoughts and intentions of the benefactor are the first to be shattered. It stands directly before this abyss, split to its core—this bottomless pit where every solid foundation and support has vanished. In the depths, it sees nothing but a common thing, a display of its own whims, a random result of its own caprice. Its spirit consists in entirely unreal imagination, a superficiality abandoned by all true spiritual meaning.

The self that is turned into a thing is, in fact, the return of reality into itself; it is a self-existence that exists for its own sake—the existential form of spirit.

The principles belonging to these realities—the thoughts of good and bad—are similarly transformed and reversed in this process; what is characterized as good is bad, and vice versa. Nobility is base and rejected, just as what is rejected as base turns into the nobility that characterizes the most highly developed form of free self-consciousness.

Looked at formally, everything is likewise in its external aspects the reverse of what it is internally for itself; and again, it is not really and in truth what it is for itself, but something other than it wants to be. Self-existence for its own sake is, strictly speaking, the loss of self; and the alienation of self is actually self-preservation.

The state of affairs brought about here is that all moments execute justice on one another all around. Each is in a condition of inherent alienation just as much as it imagines itself in its opposite, and in this way, it reverses its own nature.

Truly objective spirit, however, is precisely this unity of absolutely separate moments. A definite principle reflects the real world back into itself in a twofold form: in the particular self of consciousness as an individual, and in the pure universality of consciousness, which is thought. According to the one aspect, the mind, having thus come to itself, has directed its gaze into the world of actual reality and makes that reality its own purpose and its immediate content. From the other side, its gaze is in part turned solely upon itself and against that world of reality, and in part turned away from it toward heaven; its object is the region beyond the world.

In respect of that return into itself, the vanity of all things is its own peculiar vanity; it is itself vain. It is a self existing for its own sake, a self that knows not only how to summarize and chatter about everything, but with *esprit* and wit to capture the contradiction that lies at the heart of all reality that seems so solid, and the fixed determinations which judgment sets up; and that contradiction is their real truth. Looked at formally, it finds everything estranged from itself: self-existence is cut off from essential being (*Ansich* <note>being-in-itself</note>), and what is intended and the purpose are separated from real truth; and from both of these, again, existence-for-another—what is ostensibly put forward—is cut off from the proper meaning, the real fact, and the true intention.

It thus knows exactly how to put each moment in antithesis to every other; it knows, in short, how to express correctly the perversion that dominates all of them. #### *b*

### BELIEF AND PURE INSIGHT *

The spiritual condition of self-alienation exists as a fact within the sphere of culture. But because this whole has become estranged from itself, there lies beyond this sphere the non-actual region of pure consciousness, or thought. Its content consists of what has been reduced purely to thought; its absolute element is thinking. However, since thinking is initially the element of this sphere, consciousness merely possesses these thoughts, but it does not yet think them or know that they are thoughts. To consciousness, they appear in the form of presentations; they are objects in the form of ideas. For consciousness emerges from the sphere of actuality into that of pure consciousness, but it remains, for all intents and purposes, within the sphere of actuality and the <term>determinateness</term> that this implies. The conscious state of being rent and torn to pieces is still essentially and inherently the self-identity of pure consciousness. This is not a fact that consciousness *itself* is aware of, but is only apparent to *us* who are observing its condition. It has not yet completed the process of rising above this condition within itself; it is simply there, and it still contains within itself the opposite

This pure consciousness of Absolute Being is a consciousness in a state of alienation. Let us examine more closely the characteristics of that which is its "other"; we can only consider it in connection with this other. At first, this pure consciousness seems to have only the world of actuality standing against it. But since its nature is to flee from this actuality—and is thus characterized by opposition—it has this actuality inherent within its own being. Pure consciousness is, therefore, essentially self-alienated in its very being, and belief constitutes merely one side of it.

The other side has also already emerged. For pure consciousness is a reflection out of the world of culture in such a way that the substantial content of this sphere, as well as the separate fragments into which it falls, are shown to be what they inherently are: essential modes of spiritual life, absolutely restless processes or determinate moments that are immediately canceled in their opposite. Their essential nature, pure consciousness, is thus the simple bareness of absolute distinction—a distinction which, as it stands, is no distinction. Consequently, it is pure self-existence—not of a particular self, but an essentially universal self, whose being consists of a restless process invading and pervading the stable existence of actual fact. In it is found the certainty that immediately knows itself to be the truth; here we have pure thought in the sense of the absolute notion, with all its power of negativity, which annihilates every objective existence that would claim to stand against consciousness and transforms it into a form of conscious existence.

On the other hand, the bare consciousness of the positive element—of unbroken self-identity—finds its object in inner reality as such.

## Belief and Pure Insight

We have already seen what pure insight is on its own. Belief is the undisturbed, pure consciousness of spirit as the ultimate Reality; pure insight is the self-consciousness of spirit as that which is ultimately real. It knows what is essentially real, therefore, not *as* essence, but *as* the Absolute Self. Its aim, then, is to cancel every other kind of independence that exists outside of self-consciousness—whether that is the independence of the actually objective or of the inherently real—and to mold it into a conceptual form. It is not merely the certainty of self-conscious reason, assured that it is all truth; it knows that it is so.

However, in the form in which the concept of pure insight first encounters us, it is not yet realized. As a phase of consciousness, it consequently appears as something contingent, as something isolated and particular; its innermost constitutive nature appears as a purpose that it has to carry out and fulfill. It must begin with the intention of making pure insight universal—that is, making everything that is actual into a concept, and a concept for every self-consciousness.<note>“Kant’s philosophy is the Enlightenment adapted so as to become a philosophical method.” —Hegel, W.W. 15, p. 502.</note> The intention is pure because its content is pure insight; and this insight is likewise pure because its content is merely the absolute concept, which finds no opposition in an object and is not restricted within itself. ## II

### ENLIGHTENMENT <note>Enlightenment (*Aufklärung*) is the universalization of the principle of “pure insight,” and therefore is logically the outcome of the preceding analysis.</note>

The specific object toward which <term>pure insight</term> directs the active force of the <term>notion</term> is belief; this is a form of pure consciousness like itself and yet opposed to it in that element. But at the same time, <term>pure insight</term> has a relation to the actual world, for, like belief, it is a return from the actual world into pure consciousness. We have first of all to see how its activity is structured, as contrasted with the impure intentions and the perverted forms of insight found in the actual world. <note>Compare pages 525–533.</note>

We have touched already on the calm type of conscious life, which stands in contrast to this turmoil of alternate self-dissolution and self-evolution; it constitutes the aspect of <term>pure insight</term> and intention. This undisturbed consciousness, however, as we saw, has no special insight regarding the sphere of culture. The latter rather has the most painful feeling, and the truest insight about itself—the feeling that everything made secure crumbles to pieces, that every element of its existence is shattered to atoms, and every bone broken: moreover, it consciously expresses this feeling in words, pronounces judgment, and gives clear utterance concerning all aspects of its condition.

<summary>This page introduces Enlightenment as the application of pure insight toward belief, contrasting the calm state of pure consciousness with the turbulent and fragmented nature of the actual cultural world. It explains that while culture feels its own dissolution, pure insight remains a return to a more stable, internal consciousness.</summary>

<keywords>Enlightenment, Aufklärung, pure insight, notion, belief, consciousness, culture, self-dissolution, self-evolution</keywords>

--- Page 133 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the fragmented consciousness of culture to the unifying role of pure insight as it initiates the Enlightenment.</meta>

<page-num>547</page-num>
<header>Enlightenment</header>

Insight, therefore, can have no activity and content of its own here, and thus can only take up the formal attitude of truly apprehending this ingenious insight belonging to the world and the language it adopts. Since this language is a scattered and broken utterance and the pronouncement a fickle mood of the moment—which is quickly forgotten again, and is only known as a whole by a third consciousness—this latter can be distinguished as <term>pure insight</term> only if it gathers those several scattered traces into a universal picture, and then makes them the insight of all.

By this simple means, <term>pure insight</term> will resolve the confusion of this world. For we have found that the fragments, specific concepts, and individualities are not the essential nature of this actuality; rather, it finds its substance and support alone in the spirit which exists *qua* judging and discussing, and the interest in having a content for this <term>ratiocination</term> and parleying to deal with alone preserves the whole and the fragments into which it falls. In this language which insight adopts, its self-consciousness is still particular—a self existing for its own sake; but the emptiness of its content is at the same time the emptiness of the self knowing that content to be vain and empty. Now, since the consciousness placidly apprehending all these sparkling utterances of vanity makes a collection of the most striking and penetrating phrases, the soul that still preserves the whole—the vanity of witty criticism—goes to ruin with the other form of vanity, the previous vanity of existence. The collection shows most people a better wit, or at least shows everyone a more varied wit than their own, and shows that better knowledge and judging in general are some—

## THE STRUGGLE OF ENLIGHTENMENT WITH SUPERSTITION <note>“We live in an age of enlightenment” (Kant). Compare Hegel W W 15, introduction to “French Philosophy.”</note>

The various negative forms that consciousness adopts—the attitude of skepticism and those of theoretical and practical idealism—are inferior attitudes compared to that of pure insight and the expansion of pure insight, which is enlightenment. For pure insight is born from the substance of spirit; it knows the pure self of consciousness to be absolute and enters into conflict with the pure consciousness of the Absolute Being of all reality.

Since belief and insight are the same pure consciousness but are opposed in form—the reality in the case of belief being a thought, not a notion, and hence something absolutely opposed to self-consciousness, while the reality in the case of pure insight is the self—they are such that, *inter se*, one is the absolute negative of the other.

Appearing against one another, all content falls to belief; for in its undisturbed element of thought, each moment obtains definite subsistence. Pure insight, however, is initially without any content; it involves, rather, the complete disappearance of content. But through its negative attitude toward what it excludes, it will make itself real and give itself a content.

<vocab>Enlightenment, Superstition, consciousness, pure insight, skepticism, idealism, Absolute Being, Kant, Hegel</vocab>

<summary>This page defines Enlightenment as the expansion of pure insight and describes its fundamental conflict with religious belief. It explains that while both represent pure consciousness, they are opposites: belief treats reality as an external thought, while insight finds reality in the self.</summary>

<keywords>Enlightenment, pure insight, belief, superstition, skepticism, idealism, Absolute Being, consciousness, self-consciousness, Hegel, Kant</keywords>
