It knows belief to be opposed to insight, opposed to reason and truth. Just as, for it, belief is generally a tissue of superstitious prejudices and errors, it further sees consciousness embracing all this content as organized into a realm of error. In this realm, false insight is the general sphere of consciousness—immediate, naïvely unperturbed, and inherently unreflective. Yet all the while, this false insight does have within it the moment of self-reflection, the moment of self-consciousness, separated from its simple *naïveté*; it keeps this reflection in the background as an insight remaining by itself, and as an evil intention by which that former conscious state is fooled. That mental sphere is the victim of the deception of a priesthood, which carries out its envious vanity—jealous of being the sole possessor of insight—and carries out its other selfish ends as well. At the same time, this priesthood conspires with despotism, which takes the attitude of being the synthetic, crude (*begrifflos*) unity of the real and this ideal kingdom—a singularly amorphous and inconsistent type of being. It stands above the bad insight of the multitude and the bad intention of the priests, and even combines both of these within itself. As a result of the stupidity and confusion produced among the people by the agency of priestly deception, despotism despises both and draws for itself the advantage of undisturbed control and the fulfillment of its desires, its humors, and its whims. Yet at the same time, it is itself in this same state of murky insight; it is equally characterized by superstition and error.

Enlightenment does not attack these three forms of the enemy without distinction. For since its essential nature is pure insight, which is *per se* universal, its

Its true relation to the other extreme is the one in which it is concerned with the common and identical element in both. The aspect of individual existence isolating itself from the universal, naive consciousness is its antithesis and cannot be directly affected by it. The will of a deceiving priesthood and an oppressive despot is, therefore, not the primary object toward which it directs its activity; its object is the insight that is without will and without individualized, isolated self-existence—the notion (*Begriff*) of rational self-consciousness. This consciousness exists within the total mental sphere but is not yet present there in the fullness of its true meaning (*Begriff*). Since, however, pure insight rescues this genuinely honest form of insight, with its naive simplicity of nature, from prejudices and errors, it wrests the effective realization of its powers of deception from the hands of bad intentions. The exercise of those powers is based on the incoherent and undeveloped (*begrifflos*) consciousness of the general sphere, while isolated self-existence finds its substance in simple consciousness as a whole.

The relation of pure insight to the naive consciousness of absolute Reality now has a double aspect. On one side, pure insight is inherently one and the same with it. On the other side, however, this naive consciousness allows absolute Reality, as well as its parts, to arrange themselves at will in the simple element of its thought and to remain there; it allows them to be held only as its inherent nature and, therefore, to remain valid in an objective form. In this immanent being, however, it disowns independent existence for its own sake. We must, therefore, see how <term>pure insight</term> and pure intention maintain their negative attitude toward the "other" which they find standing in opposition.

<term>Pure insight</term> and intention, operating negatively, can only be—since their very principle is all essentiality and there is nothing outside them—the negative of themselves. As insight, therefore, it passes into the negative of pure insight and becomes untruth and unreason; and as intention, it passes into the negative of pure intention and becomes a lie and sordid impurity of purpose.

It involves itself in this contradiction by the fact that it engages in a conflict and thinks it is doing battle with some alien, external "other." It merely imagines this, for its nature as absolute negativity lies in having that otherness within its own self. The absolute <term>notion</term> is the <term>category</term>; it is the principle that <term>knowledge</term> and the object of knowledge are the same. Consequently, what pure insight expresses as its "other"—what it pronounces to be an error or a lie—can be nothing else than its own self; it can only condemn what it is. What is not rational has no truth, or what is not understood through a <term>notion</term>, conceptually determined, does not exist. Therefore, this struggle with its opposite carries the meaning of being its own realization. This consists simply in the process of unfolding its different stages and absorbing them back into itself. One part of this process is creating the distinction where the insight of reason opposes itself as an object; as long as it remains in this state, it is in conflict with itself. *As* <term>pure insight</term>, it has no content; the process of its realization consists of it becoming its own content. No other content can be given to it, because it is the <term>category</term> that has become self-conscious. But because this insight initially thinks of the content as being within its opposite, and only knows it as external content—not yet recognizing it as its own self—<term>pure insight</term> misunderstands itself within it. Therefore, the full achievement of insight is the process of learning to recognize that content as its own, even though it was originally opposed to it. However, the result will be neither the restoration of the errors it fought nor simply its original <term>notion</term>. Instead, it will be an insight that knows its own absolute <term>negation</term> to be its own true reality—to be itself. It is an insight that is a self-understanding <term>notion</term>.

This characteristic of Enlightenment’s struggle with error—fighting itself within those errors and condemning the very things it asserts—is something evident to us as observers; it is what Enlightenment and its struggle are in their underlying nature. Enlightenment, then, initially and generally conceives its object in such a way as to take it as <term>pure insight</term>. Failing to recognize itself there, it interprets it as error. In insight as such, consciousness perceives an object in such a manner that it becomes the inner being of conscious life, or becomes an object which consciousness permeates, in which consciousness maintains itself, keeps within itself, and is present to itself; and, by thus being the process of that object, it brings the object into being. It is precisely this which Enlightenment rightly declares belief to be, when Enlightenment says that the <term>Absolute Reality</term> professed by belief is a being that comes from belief’s own consciousness, is its own thought, and is something produced from and by consciousness.<note>Compare the view of God held by Fichte; also Feuerbach: *The Essence of Religion* (*Wesen der Religion*).</note> Enlightenment, consequently, interprets and declares it to be error—to be a made-up invention about the very same thing that Enlightenment itself is.

Enlightenment that seeks to teach belief this new wisdom does not tell it anything new in doing so.

For the object of belief itself is exactly this as well: namely, a pure, essential reality of its own specific consciousness. Thus, this consciousness does not consider itself lost or negated in that object, but rather places trust in it. This simply means that it finds itself there as this particular consciousness; it finds itself within the object to be self-consciousness. If I place my trust in someone, their certainty of themselves is, for me, the certainty of myself; I know my own existence through them, I know that they acknowledge it, and that it is both their purpose and their true nature. Trust, however, is belief, because its consciousness has a direct relationship with its object, and thus immediately sees that it is one with the object and within the object.

Furthermore, since whatever is an object for me is something in which I know myself, I am simultaneously present in that object in the form of another self-consciousness—that is, one which has become alienated within that object from its own specific individuality and from its natural and accidental existence, but which partly continues to be self-consciousness there, and is partly an essential consciousness just like pure insight.

In the concept of insight, there is more than just the fact that consciousness knows itself in the object it observes and finds itself there directly, without first leaving the realm of thought and then returning to itself. The concept also implies that consciousness is aware of itself as being the mediating process—aware of itself as active, as the agency of production. Through this, it arrives at the thought of this unity of the self as both self and object.

Since in this action purposiveness and end are distinguished, and pure insight also takes a negative attitude toward this action—denying itself just as it did in the other moments—it must, regarding purposiveness, appear to be stupid and unintelligent. This is because insight united with intention (the agreement of ends and means) appears to it as *an other*, as really the opposite of what insight is. Accordingly, we find that regarding purposiveness, enlightenment thinks it foolish when the believing individual seeks to obtain higher consciousness—where there is no entanglement with natural enjoyment and pleasure—by positively denying themselves natural enjoyment and pleasure. By doing so, the individual proves through their acts that they do not merely deny their contempt for these things, but rather that the contempt is quite genuine.

In the same way, enlightenment finds it foolish for consciousness to release itself from its characteristic of being absolutely individual—excluding all others and possessing its own property—by renouncing its own property; for in doing so, it shows in reality that this isolation is not really serious. It shows instead that it is something that can rise above the natural necessity of isolating itself and of denying—within this absolute isolation of its own individual existence—that others are one and the same as itself.

Pure insight finds such actions to be both purposeless and wrong. It is purposeless to renounce a pleasure and give away a possession in order to show oneself independent of pleasure and possession; therefore, in the opposite case, insight would feel obliged to proclaim that person a fool who, in order to eat, employs the method of actually eating. Insight also thinks it wrong to deny oneself a meal and give away butter and eggs—not for money, and not money for butter and eggs, but just to give them away and get no return at all. It understands a meal, or the possession of such things, to be a self’s proper object, an end for the self; therefore, it actually understands itself to be a very *impure* intention that ascribes essential value to enjoyment and possessions of this kind. As pure insight, it further maintains the necessity of rising above the condition of nature, above greed and its ways; it only finds it foolish and wrong that this supremacy should have to be demonstrated through action. In other words, this pure intention is in reality a deception which pretends to and demands an inner elevation, but declares that it is superfluous, foolish, and even wrong to be serious about the matter—to put this uplifting into concrete expression, into actual shape and form, and to demonstrate its truth.

Pure insight thus denies itself both as pure insight—for it rejects directly purposeful action—and as pure intention—for it denies the intention of proving its independence from the goals of individual existence.

This realization appeared, in the first instance, as a negative reality. Perhaps its positive reality is better established. Let us see how this stands.

When all prejudice and superstition have been banished, the question arises: what next? What is the truth that enlightenment has spread in their place? It has already expressed this positive content in its process of exterminating error, for that alienation of itself is equally its positive reality.

In dealing with what belief considers <term>Absolute Spirit</term>, it interprets whatever kind of determination it discovers there as being wood, stone, etc.—as particular, concrete things of the senses. Since in this way it conceives every characteristic in general—that is, every content and filling—to be a finite fact, a human entity, and a mental representation, <term>Absolute Being</term>, from its point of view, turns out to be a mere vacuum to which no characteristics or predicates at all can be attributed. In fact, to join such a vacuum with universal predicates would be essentially reprehensible; it is precisely through such a union that the monstrosities of superstition have been produced. Reason, pure insight, is certainly not empty itself, since its own negative is consciously present to it and serves as its content; on the contrary, it is rich in substance, but only in particularity and limitations. The enlightened function of reason, or pure insight, consists in allowing nothing of that sort to belong to <term>Absolute Reality</term>, nor attributing anything of that kind to it; this function knows well how to put itself and the wealth of finitude in their proper place and deal with the Absolute in a worthy manner.

# The Struggle of Enlightenment with Superstition 567

In contrast with this colorless, empty Reality, there stands a second aspect of the positive truth of enlightenment: the general particularity of conscious life and of everything that exists. This is a particularity excluded from an <term>absolute Being</term> and standing by itself as something entirely self-contained. Consciousness, which in its very earliest expression is <term>sense-certainty</term> and mere "opinion," returns here to this same point after the entire course of its experience. It is once again a *knowledge* of what is the pure negative of itself—a knowledge of sensory things, meaning existing entities that stand in indifference toward its own <term>self-existence</term>. 

But here, it is not an *immediate*, naive consciousness; it has *become* immediate to itself. While it was at first a victim of every sort of entanglement into which its gradual unfolding plunged it, and is now led back to its first form by pure insight, it has arrived at this first state as the result and outcome of the process. This <term>sense-certainty</term>, resting as it does on an insight into the nothingness of all other forms of consciousness—and therefore the nothingness of whatever lies beyond sensory experience—is no longer a mere "opinion"; it is, instead, absolute truth. 

This nothingness of everything that transcends the senses is undoubtedly merely a negative proof of this truth. But no other proof is admissible or possible, for the positive truth of sensory experience in itself is simply the unmediated self-existence of the <term>notion</term> itself *as* an object, and an object in the form of otherness. The positive truth is that it is absolutely certain to every consciousness that it exists, that there are other real things outside it, and that in its naive existence, both consciousness and these things are in and for themselves, or absolute.

<summary>Enlightenment concludes that because the Absolute is an empty void, the only remaining certain truth is sensory experience and the existence of particular, finite things. Consciousness returns to its starting point of sense-certainty, but now views it as an absolute truth rather than a mere opinion.</summary>

# Phenomenology of Mind

Lastly, the third moment of the truth of enlightenment is the relationship of particular entities to <term>Absolute Being</term>; it is the relationship of the first two moments to one another. Insight, as the pure insight into what is identical or unrestricted, also transcends what is different or diverse—that is, it transcends finite reality, or transcends itself in the form of mere otherness. It considers the "beyond" of this otherness to be a void, to which it then relates the facts of the senses. In defining this relationship, neither of the two terms enters the relationship as its actual content; for one is the void, and therefore content can only be obtained through the other—through sensory reality. 

However, the form that this relationship takes—to which the aspect of intrinsic and essential being (<term>Ansich</term>) contributes—can be shaped however we please. This is because the form is something inherently and essentially negative, and therefore something self-contradictory, being both existence and nothingness, the intrinsic and essential (<term>Ansich</term>) as well as its opposite. Or, to put it another way, the relationship of reality to an essential being that exists as a "beyond" is as much a denial of that reality as it is an affirmation of it. 

Finite realities can, therefore, properly speaking, be treated in whatever way people need to use them. Sensory facts are thus sometimes related positively to the Absolute as something essential (<term>Ansich</term>), and sensory reality is itself seen as essential in its own right; the Absolute creates, fosters, and cherishes them. Then, again, they are related to it as an opposite—that is, to their own non-existence; in this case, they are not something essential, but exist only for the sake of another. While in the previous mode of consciousness the concepts involved in this opposition took the form of "good" and "bad," in the case of pure insight they pass into the more

Enlightenment is as much an abomination to belief as is its negative attitude toward it. This enlightened insight into absolute Reality, which sees nothing in it but absolute Reality itself—the *être suprême* (supreme being) or the great Void—and its intention to find that everything in its immediate existence is inherently real (*an sich*) or good, and finally to find the relation of the particular conscious entity to the Absolute Being (Religion) summed up entirely in the concept of usefulness—all this is, for belief, utterly and simply revolting. This special and peculiar wisdom of Enlightenment necessarily seems to the believing mind to be sheer dullness and a confession of emptiness. This is because it consists in knowing nothing of absolute Being, or—what amounts to the same thing—in knowing only this entirely accurate platitude regarding it: that it is merely absolute Being. Furthermore, it consists in knowing nothing but finitude, taking this to be the truth, and thinking that this knowledge about finitude *as* truth is the highest knowledge attainable.

Belief has a divine right against Enlightenment: the right of absolute self-identity or of pure thought. It finds itself utterly wronged by Enlightenment, for Enlightenment distorts all of belief's elements and makes them something quite different from what they are within belief itself. Enlightenment, on the other hand, has merely a human right against belief and can only put in a human claim for its own truth. The wrong it commits is the right of disunion and discordance; it consists in perverting and altering—a right that belongs to the nature of self-consciousness in opposition to the simple, ultimate essence or thought. Insight, therefore, has and retains its right against belief because it validates within belief what is necessary to belief itself, and what belief contains within it.

At first, Enlightenment asserts the moment of the <term>notion</term> to be an act of consciousness; it maintains in the face of belief that the absolute Reality belief accepts is a Reality of the believer's consciousness *as* a self, or that this absolute Reality is produced through consciousness. Finally, regarding the view Enlightenment takes of the action of belief, the rejection of enjoyment and possessions is looked upon as wrong and pointless.

As to the wrong thus done, Enlightenment preserves the harmony of the believing attitude in this: that belief acknowledges the actual reality of owning property, keeping hold of it, and enjoying it. In insisting on its property, it behaves with all the more stubborn independence and exclusiveness; and in its enjoyment, it behaves with all the more frank self-abandonment, since its religious act of giving up pleasure and property takes effect beyond the region of this reality, and purchases for it the freedom to do as it likes as far as that other sphere is concerned. As for purposiveness, Enlightenment finds it pointless and foolish to throw away a possession in order to feel and to prove oneself to be free from all possession, or to renounce *an* enjoyment in order to think and demonstrate that one is rid of all enjoyment. The spirit that quietly works and weaves within itself without further distinctions has thus passed into itself, moving beyond consciousness, which has once again reached clarity regarding itself. The real essence is divided here in such a way that, to begin with, it belongs to two specifically distinct modes of thinking. In part, the real must contain distinction within itself; in part, just by doing so, both ways of considering it merge into one. The universal common to both is the abstraction of pure self-thinking, of pure movement within the self. This simple motion of rotating on its own axis is bound to resolve itself into separate moments, because it is itself only motion by distinguishing its own moments. This distinguishing of the moments leaves the unmoved [unity] behind as the empty shell of pure being, which is no longer actual thought and has no more life within it; for *qua* distinction, this process is the entire content. The process, which thus places itself outside that unity, thereby constitutes the shifting change—a change that does not return into itself—of the moments of <term>being-in-itself</term>, of <term>being-for-another</term>, and of <term>being-for-self</term>. Pure insight, as we have seen, is the living <term>concept</term> itself, the very same pure personality. It distinguishes itself within itself in such a way that each of the distinct elements is itself a pure concept—meaning it is *by that very fact* not distinct. It is simple, undifferentiated, pure self-consciousness, which exists for itself as well as in itself within an immediate unity. Its inherent being—its <term>being-in-itself</term>—is therefore not fixed or permanent; instead, as it is distinguished, it immediately ceases to be something distinct.

However, a being of that kind—which is immediately without support and cannot stand on its own—has no inherent existence or <term>being-in-itself</term>. It exists essentially for something else, which is the power that consumes and absorbs it. But this second moment, which is opposed to the first, also disappears immediately, just like the first. Or rather, *as* a being that exists merely for another, it is the very process of disappearing itself, and is clearly affirmed as a being that has returned into itself—as <term>being-for-self</term>. Yet this simple being-for-self, *as* self-identity, is instead an objective being, and is thus for another.

This nature of pure insight, as it unfolds and makes its moments explicit—in other words, insight *as an object*—finds expression in the **useful** or the **profitable**. What is useful is a thing, something that exists in itself; yet this <term>being-in-itself</term> is at the same time only a pure moment. Consequently, it exists absolutely for something else, but it exists for another only insofar as it is in itself. These opposite moments return into the indivisible unity of <term>being-for-self</term>.

Because the useful still appears before insight in the form of an object, insight has a world—not indeed a world that is any longer entirely independent and self-contained, but still a world nonetheless, which it distinguishes from itself. However, since the opposites have emerged at the summit of the <term>concept</term>, the next step will be for them to collide with one another and for <term>Enlightenment</term> to experience the fruits of its deeds.

When we look at the object reached in relation to this entire sphere of <term>spiritual life</term>, we find the actual world of culture summed up in the vanity of <term>self-consciousness</term>—in independent self-existence, whose content is drawn from the confusion characteristic of culture, and which is still the individual <term>concept</term>, not yet the self-conscious (*für sich*) universal <term>concept</term>. Returned into itself, however, that individual <term>concept</term> is <term>pure insight</term>—pure consciousness *as* the pure self or

### III

## ABSOLUTE FREEDOM AND TERROR*

Consciousness has found its concept in the principle of utility. But that concept is still partly an object, and for that very reason, it is still a purpose that consciousness does not yet find itself immediately possessing. Utility or usefulness is still a predicate of the object, not a subject—not its immediate and sole reality. It is the same situation that appeared before, when we found that self-existence (being-for-self) had not yet shown itself to be the substance of the other moments. This is a process by which the useful would be primarily nothing other than the self of consciousness, and consciousness would thereby possess it.

This resumption of the form of objectivity which characterizes the useful has, however, already taken effect implicitly. As the outcome of this inherent internal revolution, the actual revolution of concrete reality comes to light: the new mode of conscious life—absolute freedom.

This is because, in fact, there is nothing here but an empty appearance of objectivity separating self-consciousness from actual possession. For, in part, all the worth and permanence of the various specific members of the organization of the world of reality and belief have, as a whole, returned into this simple

determination, which is their foundation and their indwelling spirit. In part, however, this specific element has nothing uniquely its own left for itself; it is instead pure metaphysics, a pure concept, or the knowledge of self-consciousness. That is to say, from the inherent and specific nature of the useful *as* an object, consciousness learns that its inherent nature—its "being-in-itself"—is essentially a "being for another." Mere being by itself, since it lacks a self, is ultimately and in truth a passive entity, or something that exists for another self. The object, however, is present to consciousness in this abstract form of purely internal being, of pure being-in-itself; for consciousness is the activity of pure insight, the separate moments of which take the pure form of concepts.

Self-existence, or "being-for-self"—into which "being for another" returns—is the self. However, this is not a self belonging to what is called an "object," a self all its own and different from the ego. For consciousness, as pure insight, is not an individual self against which the object could stand as if it had a self of its own. Instead, it is the pure concept, the self gazing into the self, the literal and absolute seeing of itself doubled. This certainty of itself is the universal subject, and its concept, knowing itself, is the essential being of all reality. If the useful were merely the shifting change of these moments, without returning into its own proper unity, and was thus still an object for knowledge to deal with, it ceases to be that now. For knowing is itself the process and movement of those abstract moments; it is the universal self—the self of itself as well as of the object—and, being universal, it is the unity of this process, a unity that returns into itself.

It is conscious of its pure personality and, with that, of all spiritual reality; and all reality is solely spirituality. For this consciousness, the world is absolutely its own will, and this will is a universal will. And further, this will is not the empty thought of a will, which is formed by giving a silent agreement, or an agreement through a representative—a mere symbol of willing. Instead, it is a concretely embodied universal will, the will of all individuals as such. For will is in itself the consciousness of personality belonging to every single person; and it must exist as this true, concrete, actual will, as the self-conscious essential being of each and every personality, so that each single and undivided person does everything. Thus, what appears to be done by the whole is simultaneously and consciously the deed of every single individual.

This undivided substance of absolute freedom places itself on the throne of the world, without any power being able to offer effective resistance. For since, in very truth, consciousness alone is the element which provides spiritual beings or powers with their substance, their entire system—which is organized and maintained through division into separate spheres and distinct wholes—collapses into a single whole once the individual consciousness perceives the object as having no other nature than that of self-conscious-

Just as individual self-consciousness does not find itself in this universal work of absolute freedom as an existing substance, it finds itself just as little in the specific deeds and individual acts of will performed by this substance. For the universal to pass into a deed, it must gather itself into the single unity of individuality and place an individual consciousness at the forefront; for the universal will is an actual concrete will only in a self that is single and one. As a result, however, all other individuals are excluded from the whole of this deed and have only a restricted share in it, so that the deed would not be a deed of truly universal self-consciousness.

Universal freedom can thus produce neither a positive achievement nor a deed; there is left for it only negative action; it is merely the rage and fury of disappearance and destruction.

But the highest reality of all—and the reality most opposed to absolute freedom, or rather the sole object it is yet to become aware of—is the freedom and singleness of actual self-consciousness itself. For that universality which does not let itself attain the reality of organic differentiation, and whose purpose is to maintain itself in unbroken continuity, distinguishes itself within itself all the while, because it is a process or consciousness in general. Moreover, on account of its own peculiar abstraction, it divides itself into extremes that are equally abstract: into the cold, unbending, bare universality, and the hard, discrete, absolute rigidity and stubborn atomic singleness of actual self-consciousness. That meaningless death, the insubstantial, empty negativity of the self, turns, in its inner constitutive principle, into absolute positivity. For consciousness, the immediate unity of itself with the universal will—its demand to see and find itself as a specific, particular focus within the universal will—is changed and converted into the absolutely opposite experience. What it loses there is abstract being, the immediate existence of that insubstantial focus; and this vanished immediacy is the universal will as such, which it now knows itself to be, insofar as it is a transcended and canceled immediacy—insofar as it is pure knowledge or pure will. By this means, it knows that will to be itself, and knows itself to be essential reality; but not as the immediate essence, not as the will as revolutionary...

## SPIRIT IN THE CONDITION OF BEING CERTAIN OF ITSELF: MORALITY

The following section deals with the final and highest stage in the life of finite spiritual experience as realized in the concrete form of a historical society. Here, the substance of the social order is the actual content of the self-conscious individual; that substance has been internalized as a subject. We have, therefore, a self-contained spiritual subject. The conflict found in the realms of culture and enlightenment is overcome by the self knowing and realizing itself as a completely universal, self-determining free will—its world is within itself, and the self is its own world. Each individual reflects the whole (the totality of social life) within themselves so perfectly that what they do is clearly the work of the whole as much as it is their own doing. This sphere of spiritual existence is Morality: the self-sufficient spiritual order of the finite spirit as an individual. The meaning assigned to “morality” here is the one expressed by Kant when he says that morality is “the relation of actions to the autonomy of the will—that is, to the possibility of universal legislation through maxims of the will.” In other words, all the universality that forms the relationships between finite spirits in a society is epitomized in the soul of the acting individual, who can thus quite legitimately look upon themselves as the self-regulating source of all universal conditions for action.

It is inevitable that such a concrete mode of experience should have various aspects and should pass through various stages in the process of fully realizing its nature. The individual may place exclusive stress on the self-completeness they possess by being the source and origin of their own laws. This self-legislating function, precisely because it carries with it the sense of universality, may appear so supremely important that all the actual details of their life come to be treated as external, indifferent, and accidental. These details, no doubt, are essential to give body and substance to one's spiritual individuality, but the universality of the will so far transcends every detail of content that it seems, by itself, to be the sole and self-sufficient reality of one’s being. The content of their life only enters into consideration as an element to be regulated and made to conform to the universal: the relation so constituted between content and universal is

## SPIRIT IN THE CONDITION OF BEING CERTAIN OF ITSELF: MORALITY

The ethical order of the community reached its completion and its truth in the type of spirit existing in mere solitude and isolation within it—the individual self. This legal person, however, finds its substance and its fulfillment outside of that ethical order. The process of the world of culture and belief removes this abstraction of a mere person; and by the completion of the process of alienation, by reaching the furthest point of abstraction, the self of spirit finds that substance first becomes the universal will, and finally its own possession. Here, then, knowledge seems at last to have become entirely at one with the truth it pursues; for its truth is this knowledge itself. All opposition between the two sides has disappeared, and that, too, not just *for us* (who are tracing the process), and not merely implicitly, but actually *for self-consciousness itself*. That is to say, knowledge itself has gained mastery over the opposition which consciousness had to face. This is based on the opposition between the certainty of the self and the object. Now, however, the object for it is the certainty of self, which is knowledge: just as the certainty of itself as such no longer has goals of its own, is no longer conditioned or defined, but is pure knowledge.

Self-consciousness now, therefore, takes the knowledge of itself to be the substance itself. This substance is, for it, at once immediate and absolutely mediated in one

But it is not *character*, just as that ethical consciousness—which because of its immediacy is a specific type of spirit—belongs merely to one of the essential features of ethical life and has the unique quality of not being conscious, explicit knowledge. It is, again, absolute mediation, as it involves the conscious processes of culture and belief; for it is essentially the movement of the self’s life to transcend the abstract form of immediate existence and become consciously universal—and yet to do so neither by simply alienating and tearing itself and reality apart, nor by fleeing from it. Rather, it is directly and immediately present in its very substance; for this substance is its knowledge—the pure certainty of self having become transparently visible. And this very immediacy, which constitutes its actual reality, is the entire actuality. For the immediate is being, and *as* pure immediacy—an immediacy made transparent by thoroughgoing negation—this immediacy is pure being, is being in general, is all being.

Absolute essential Being is, therefore, not limited to being the simple essence of thought; it is all actuality, and this actuality exists merely as knowledge. Whatever consciousness did not know would have no meaning and could have no power in its life. All objectivity, the entire world, has withdrawn into its self-conscious, knowing will. It is absolutely free because it knows its freedom; and this very knowledge of its freedom is its substance, its purpose, and its one and only content.

## THE MORAL VIEW OF THE WORLD

Self-consciousness knows and accepts duty as the Absolute. It is bound by that alone, and this substance is its own conscious life, pure and simple; duty cannot, for it, take on the form of something alien and external. However, when thus enclosed and confined within itself, moral self-consciousness is not yet affirmed and perceived as *consciousness.*<note>That is, there is not the opposition of an object to a subject which consciousness requires.</note> The object is immediate knowledge and, because it is purely permeated by the self, it is not an *object.* But, since this knowledge is essentially *mediation* and *negativity,* its very concept implies a relation to some *otherness*; and thus it is consciousness. Because duty constitutes its sole essential purpose and objective content, this "other" is a reality completely devoid of significance for consciousness. But again, because this consciousness is so entirely confined within itself, it adopts a perfectly free and detached attitude toward this otherness. Therefore, the existence of this "other" is an existence completely independent of self-consciousness, relating only to itself in a similar way. The freer self-consciousness becomes, the freer also is the negative object of its consciousness. The object is thus a complete world within itself, with an individuality of

Starting from a specific character of this kind, a moral outlook or point of view is formed and established. This view consists in a process of relating the implicit aspect of morality (*moralisches Ansichseyn*) and the explicit aspect (*moralisches Fürsichseyn*). This relationship presupposes both a complete mutual indifference and a distinct independence between nature and moral purposes and activity. On the other hand, it also presupposes a conscious sense of duty as the only essential fact, and views nature as entirely lacking independence and essential significance of its own. The point of view or attitude of the moral life consists in the development of these moments, which are involved in this relationship of such entirely antithetical and contradictory assumptions.

To begin with, then, the moral consciousness in general is assumed. It takes duty to be the essential reality: it is itself actual and active, and in its actuality and action, it fulfills duty. But at the same time, this moral consciousness is confronted by the assumed freedom of nature: it learns through experience that nature is not concerned with providing consciousness with a sense of unity between its own reality and that of nature. # The Moral View of the World

Moral consciousness, *as* the mere and simple knowledge and willing of pure duty, is brought into relationship with the diverse reality presented by various cases through the process of acting upon an object opposed to that abstract simplicity. As a result, it adopts a moral attitude that is varied and complex. From this arises, regarding content, the general plurality of laws, and regarding form, the contradictory forces of intelligent, knowing consciousness and of a being without consciousness.

To begin with, regarding the plurality of duties, it is only the aspect of pure or simple duty within them that generally holds significance for moral consciousness. The many duties, *as* many, are specific and therefore are not, in themselves, sacred to moral consciousness. At the same time, however, because they are necessary by the very nature of action—which involves a diverse reality and thus diverse types of moral attitudes—these many duties must be seen as having a substantial existence and value. Furthermore, since they can only exist within a moral consciousness, they must exist in a consciousness other than the one for which only pure, simple duty is sacred and self-sufficient.

It is thus postulated that another consciousness exists which makes them sacred, or which recognizes them as duties and wills them to be so. The first consciousness maintains that pure duty is indifferent to all specific content, and duty

Consequently, this consciousness is one in which the universal and the particular are completely unified; its essential principle is thus the same as the principle of the harmony between morality and happiness. For this opposition between morality and happiness similarly expresses the separation of the self-identical moral consciousness from the reality which, <term>as</term> a diverse existence, opposes and conflicts with the simple nature of duty. 

However, while the first postulate merely expresses the objective, existential harmony between morality and nature—because nature is there the negative of self-consciousness, the aspect of existence—this inherent harmony is now essentially affirmed as a mode of consciousness. For existence now appears as the content of duty, as the element in a specific duty that gives it its particular character. This internal harmony is thus the unity of elements which, <term>as</term> simple ultimate elements, are essentially created by thought and, therefore, cannot exist except within a consciousness. This latter consciousness now becomes a master and ruler of the world, who brings about the harmony of morality and happiness and, at the same time, makes the various duties sacred. To make these duties sacred means that the consciousness of pure duty cannot immediately and directly accept a specific duty as sacred; but because a specific duty,

# The Moral View of the World

owing to the nature of concrete action, which is something specific and definite, is nevertheless necessary, its necessity falls outside that consciousness and exists within another consciousness. This other consciousness thus mediates or connects specific and pure duty, and is the reason why that specific duty also has validity.

In the concrete act, however, consciousness proceeds to work as this particular self, as a completely individual entity: it directs its activity toward actual reality as such and takes this as its purpose, for it wants to perform something definite. “Duty in general” thus falls outside it and within another being, which is the consciousness and sacred lawgiver of pure duty. The consciousness that acts, precisely because it acts, accepts the other consciousness—that of pure duty—and admits its validity immediately; this pure duty is thus a content of another consciousness, and it is only indirectly or in a mediated way sacred for the active consciousness, namely, by virtue of this other consciousness.

Because it is established in this manner that the validity—the binding nature—of duty as something wholly and absolutely sacred falls outside the actual consciousness, the latter thereby stands altogether on one side as an incomplete moral consciousness. Just as, in regard to its *knowledge*, it is aware of itself as that whose knowledge and conviction are incomplete and contingent; in the same way, as regards its *willing*, it feels itself to be that whose purposes are affected by sensory feelings. On account of its “unworthiness,” therefore, it cannot look on happiness as something necessary, but as something contingent, and can only expect happiness as the result of “grace.”

As far as its pure will and knowledge are concerned, this is held to be the essential truth. In principle, therefore, so far as the <term>notion</term> is opposed to <term>actual reality</term>—in other words, in *thought*—it is perfect. The absolute truth <note>duty</note> is, however, simply this object of thought, and is something postulated beyond the actual. It is therefore the thought in which morally imperfect knowledge and will are held to be perfect; and—since it acknowledges this imperfection to be significant—it is the thought in which happiness is consequently distributed according to "<term>worthiness</term>," that is, according to the "<term>merit</term>" ascribed to it.

This completes the meaning of the moral attitude. For in the conception of <term>moral self-consciousness</term>, the two aspects, <term>pure duty</term> and <term>actual reality</term>, are joined in a single unity. Because of this, each is presented not as something complete in itself, but as a "moment," or as something cancelled and <term>transcended</term>. This becomes clearly explicit in the final phase of the moral attitude or point of view. As we saw there, consciousness places pure duty in a form of being other than its own consciousness; that is, it regards pure duty partly as something ideally presented, and partly as what does not hold good by itself—indeed, the non-moral is instead what is held to be perfect. In the same way, it affirms itself to be that whose <term>actuality</term>, because it does not conform to duty, is transcended; as it is <term>transcended</term>, or within the ideal representation of what is absolute <note>pure duty</note>, it no longer contradicts morality.

In composing this opposition, it does not relate and compare the elements with one another, but proceeds forward on its own course of development without being the connecting principle of those moments. Its procedure is thus merely that of thinking, not conceiving; it operates through thoughts, not <term>notions</term> <note>often translated as "concepts" in modern philosophical contexts</note>. Consequently, it does not yet find the object of its actual consciousness to be transparently clear to itself; it is not the absolute notion, which alone grasps otherness as such—its absolute opposite—as its very self. Its own reality, as well as all objective reality, is no doubt held to be something unessential; but its freedom is that of pure thought, in opposition to which nature has also emerged as something equally free. Because both are found within it in the same manner—both the freedom which belongs to external being and the inclusion of this existence within consciousness—its object becomes an existing object which is, at the same time, merely a thought-product. In the final phase of its attitude or point of view, the content is essentially constituted so that its being has the character of something presented, an idea; and this union of being and thinking is expressed as what it actually is, namely—<term>Presentation</term>.

# Phenomenology of Mind

<margin>A handwritten pencil bracket and checkmark delineate the first paragraph.</margin>

The first stage, which forms the starting point, is actual moral self-consciousness, or the fact that such a self-consciousness exists at all. For the <term>notion</term> <note>often translated as "concept"</note> establishes moral self-consciousness in a way that, for it, all reality in general has essential being only insofar as that reality conforms with duty; and that notion establishes this essential element as knowledge—that is, in immediate unity with the actual self. This unity is thus itself actual; it is an actual moral consciousness. The latter, now, *as* consciousness, presents its content to itself as an object—namely, as the final purpose of the world, as the harmony of morality with all reality. However, since it represents this unity as an object and is not yet the complete notion (which grasps the object as such), this unity is taken to be something negative toward or opposed to self-consciousness. That is, the unity falls outside it as something beyond its actual reality, but at the same time it is of such a nature as to also exist, even if it is merely thought of.

This self-consciousness, which *as* self-consciousness is something other than the object, thus finds itself lacking harmony between the consciousness of duty and actual reality—a reality, too, which is its own. Consequently, the proposition now runs: “there is no morally complete actual self-consciousness”; and, since what is moral only exists in the long run insofar as it is complete—for duty is the pure, unadulterated, ultimate element (<term>Ansich</term> <note>the "in-itself"</note>), and morality consists merely in conforming to this pure principle—the second proposition runs: “there is no morally actual existence at all.”

Since, however, in the third place, it is a self, it is inherently the unity of duty and actual reality. This

# The Moral View of the World

Unity thus becomes its object as completed morality—but as something beyond its actual reality, and yet a “beyond” which still ought to be real.

In this final stage and last expression of the synthetic unity of the first two propositions, self-conscious reality, as well as duty, is only affirmed as a transcended or superseded moment. For neither of them is alone, and neither is isolated; on the contrary, these factors, whose essential characteristic lies in being free from one another, are thus, in that unity, no longer free from the other; each is transcended. Hence, regarding content, they become as such an object; each of them holds good for the other. Regarding form, they become such that this interchange on their part is, at the same time, merely an idea—it is merely ideally presented. Or, again, the actually non-moral, because it is simultaneously pure thought and elevated above its own actual reality, is in idea *still* moral and is taken to be entirely sufficient. In this way, the first proposition—that there is a moral self-consciousness—is reinstated, but bound up with the second—that there is *none*. That is to say, there is one, but merely in idea. In other words, there is indeed none, but it is nonetheless allowed by some other consciousness to pass for one.

## DISSEMBLANCE

[The first stage, as it stands, fails to do complete justice to the full meaning of morality. Both elements in the spiritually complete individual are essential, and each must be recognized. The universal must be objectified in nature ("external nature" and "sensibility"), and nature must be subjectivized in spirit. Therefore, another condition or stage of the moral consciousness is found where the equal value of the elements of the moral consciousness is admitted, without these elements being completely fused into a single and total attitude. The universal is realized in many ways and forms, and each is accepted in turn as the true moral reality. The mind passes from one to the other; when one is accepted, the other is set aside. The moral consciousness tries, so to speak, to hide from itself the endless diversity of its appearances, simply because it clings tenaciously to the idea that its inherent self-completeness is a unity *per se* which can only admit diversity on sufferance. Previously, it eliminated all diversity by eliminating the source of diversity—nature. Here, it is forced to admit diversity, and yet cannot give up the claim to be an abstract, single unity independent of difference. Thus, its condition here is a mixture of self-realization and self-sophistication—a condition which Hegel characterizes as "Dissemblance," and which borders upon and may pass into "Hypocrisy." Hegel regards this attitude as the inevitable outcome of the preceding stage.]

# DISSEMBLANCE *

<note>Dissemblance (*Verstellung*): It is not possible to convey exactly in English the wordplay involved in Hegel’s interpretation of the state of mind discussed here. In the course of his analysis, Hegel uses the meaning implied in the general term “*stellen*” (to place or set) to explain, by contrast, the specific nuance of the purely moral attitude conveyed by the term *verstellen* (to displace, disguise, or dissemble).</note>

In the moral attitude of experience, we see on one side that consciousness itself produces its object in a conscious way. We find that it neither encounters the object as something external, nor does the object appear before it in an unconscious manner. Rather, consciousness proceeds throughout on a specific basis, and from this, it establishes objective reality. It thus recognizes this objective element as itself, for it is aware of itself as the active agent producing this object. Consequently, it seems to attain its peace and satisfaction here; this can only be found where consciousness no longer needs to go beyond its object, because the object no longer goes beyond it. On the other side, however, it actually places the object outside itself, as something beyond its own reach. Yet this latter self-contained entity is at the same time positioned as something that is not detached from self-consciousness, but exists truly on behalf of and by means of it.

The moral attitude is, therefore, in fact nothing other than the developed expression of this fundamental contradiction in its various aspects. It is—to use a Kantian phrase which is most appropriate here—a “perfect

But, in the way it has now set up this second moment, it also “shifts” (*verstellt*) this again, and really makes the opposite the essential element. At the same time, it is conscious of its contradiction in this displacement, for it passes from one moment, in its immediate relation to this very moment, right over to the opposite. Because a moment has no reality for it at all, it *affirms* that very moment as real; or, what comes to the same thing, in order to assert one moment as existing *per se*, it asserts the opposite as existing *per se*. It thereby confesses that, as a matter of fact, it is in earnest about neither of them. We must look at the various moments of this fraudulent process more closely.

Let us first allow the assumption that there is an actual moral consciousness to rest on its own basis, because the assumption is not directly made with reference to something preceding; and let us turn to the harmony of morality and nature—the first postulate. It is to be immanent, not explicitly for actual conscious life, and not really present; the present is rather simply the contradiction between the two. In the present, morality is taken to be something at hand, and actual reality to be so situated or “placed” that it is not in harmony with morality. # Dissemblance

At the same time, the performance of the action is a conscious fact; it is the "presence" of this unity of reality and purpose. Action thus, as a fact, directly fulfills what it was claimed could not take place at all; it fulfills what was meant to be merely a postulate, supposed to lie merely "beyond." Consciousness, therefore, expresses through its deed that it is not serious about making the postulate, since the meaning of acting is really that it creates a present fact out of what was not supposed to exist in the present. And, since the harmony is postulated for the sake of the action—because what is to become actual through action must *be* implicit, otherwise the reality would not be possible—the connection of action with the postulate is constructed such that, for the sake of the action (that is, for the sake of the actual harmony of purpose and reality), this harmony is presented as not actual, as far away, as "beyond."

On that mode of interpretation, then, there has arisen an essential situation which renders moral action superfluous and in which moral action does not take place at all. That this moral completion is not taken seriously is directly expressed by consciousness in the fact that it shifts this completion away into infinity—that is, it asserts that the completion is never completed.

Thus, it is really only the middle state of being incomplete that is admitted to have any value: a state which, nevertheless, at least ought to be one of progress toward completion. Yet it cannot be so; for advancing in morality would mean approaching its annihilation and disappearance. For the goal would be the nothingness mentioned above, the abolition of morality and consciousness itself; but to come ever nearer and nearer to nothing means to decrease. Besides, "advancing" would generally, in the same way as "decreasing," introduce distinctions of quantity into morality; but these are quite inadmissible in such a sphere. In morality *quâ* mode of consciousness which takes the ethical end to be pure duty, we cannot think at all of difference, least of all of the superficial difference of quantity: there is only one virtue, only one pure duty, only one morality.

Since, then, it is not moral completion that is taken seriously, but rather the middle state—that is, as just explained, the condition of no morality—we thus come by another way back to the content of the first postulate. For we cannot perceive how happiness is to be demanded for this moral consciousness on the ground of its worthiness to be happy. It is well aware of its not being complete, and cannot, therefore, in point of fact, demand happiness as a desert, as something of

One may pretend to have found through experience that, in the actual present, the person who is moral often fares poorly, while the person who is not often succeeds. Yet the middle state of incomplete morality—the condition that has proven to be the essential one—shows clearly that this perception of morality faring poorly (this "experience" that is claimed to be real but is not) is merely a *dissemblance* of the actual facts of the case. For since morality is not completed—that is, since morality, in point of fact, *is not*—how can there be any experience of morality faring badly?

Since it has also been revealed that the issue at hand concerns happiness alone, it is manifest that when making the judgment, “the man who has no morality succeeds,” there was no intention to convey that there is something wrong in such a case. The characterization of an individual as someone devoid of morality necessarily falls apart when morality in general is incomplete; such a description rests, indeed, on pure whim. Morality, then, in the moral consciousness, is not completed. This is what is now established. But its essence consists in being merely what is complete, and thus pure morality: incomplete morality is, therefore, impure; in other words, it is Immorality. Morality itself thus exists in a being other than the actual concrete consciousness. This other is a holy moral legislator.

Morality which is not completed in consciousness—the morality that is the reason for making those postulates—means, in the first instance, that morality, when it is set up as actual in consciousness, stands in relation to something else, to an existence. Thus, it preserves and implies otherness or distinction, from which arises a manifold plurality of moral commands. The moral self-consciousness at the same time, however, looks on these many duties as unessential; for it is concerned with merely the one pure duty, and this plurality of duties—so far as they are specific duties—has no true reality for self-consciousness. They can thus have their real truth accepted only in another consciousness, and they are (what they are not for the actual moral self-consciousness) sacred through a holy law-giver.

But this, too, is again merely a dissembling of the actual fact. For moral self-consciousness is to itself...

Moral consciousness, further, is not really serious in allowing something to be made sacred by another consciousness than its own. It is thus just as little in earnest in treating this other being as a holy being; for this would mean that something within it was to attain an essential significance which, for the moral consciousness—that is, in itself—has none.

If the sacred being was postulated so that duty might have binding validity within the moral consciousness—not *as* pure duty, but as a plurality of specific duties—then this must again be dissembled, and the other being must be solely sacred insofar as only pure duty has binding validity within the moral consciousness. Pure duty also has, in point of fact, validity and obligation only in another being, not in the moral consciousness. Although pure morality seems alone to hold good within the latter, still this must be corrected in another form, for it is, at the same time, a natural consciousness. Morality is, in it, affected and conditioned by sensibility, and thus is not by itself self-contained, but a contingent result of free will; in it, however, *as* pure will, morality is a contingency of knowledge. Taken by itself, therefore, morality is in another being; it is self-complete only in another reality than the actual moral consciousness.

The moral consciousness accounts for its incompleteness by the fact that morality, in its case, has a positive relation to nature and sensibility, since it holds an essential moment of morality to be that morality should have simply and solely a negative relation toward nature and sensibility. The pure moral being, on the other hand, because it is far above the struggle with nature and sense, does not stand in a negative relation to them. This other being, so purely and entirely moral, is again, therefore, a mere dissemblance of the actual fact, and has to be given up.

In this purely moral being, however, the moments of the contradiction, in which this synthetic ideational process is carried on, come closer together. So, likewise, do the opposites taken up alternately—now this and *also* that, and *also* the other—opposites which are allowed to follow one after the other, with one opposite constantly set aside by another, yet without these ideas ever being brought together. So close do they come, that consciousness here has to give up its moral view of the world and retreat within itself.

This pure morality, then, has its real existence in some other being. But such reality means nothing other than that morality is self-complete here, in itself and for itself—*for itself*, meaning it is the morality of a consciousness; *in itself*, meaning it has existence and actuality.

In that first incomplete consciousness, morality is not realized or carried out. It exists there as something inherent and implicit, in the sense of being a mere <term>thought-element</term>; for it is associated with nature and sensibility, and with the actuality of [external] existence and conscious life, which constitutes its content; yet nature and sensibility are morally nothing. In the second being, morality is present as completed, and not in the form of an unrealized <term>thought-element</term>. But this completion consists precisely in the fact that morality has reality in a consciousness—in the sense of a free reality and objective existence in general—and is not something empty, but filled out and full of content. That is to say, the completion of morality is found in this: that what was characterized a moment ago as morally nothing is found present in and inherent to morality. At one time, it is to have validity simply and solely as the unrealized <term>thought-element</term>, a product of pure abstraction; but, on the other hand, it is just as

certainly to have no validity at all in this form: its true nature consists in being opposed to reality, completely detached from it and empty, and then again in being actual reality.

The syncretism, or fusion, of these contradictions, which is expressed *at length* in the moral attitude of experience, collapses internally. This happens because the distinction on which it rests—the distinction between something that must be thought and stated as a necessity, yet is simultaneously not essential—passes into a distinction that no longer exists even in words. What is ultimately affirmed to be something with different aspects—to be both nothing and also real—is one and the same thing: existence and reality. And what is supposed to be absolute only as something beyond actual existence and actual consciousness, yet at the same time exists only in consciousness (and so, *as* a "beyond," is nothing at all)—this absolute is pure duty and the knowledge that pure duty is essentially real. The consciousness that makes this distinction (which is no distinction at all), which declares actuality to be simultaneously nothing and real, pronounces pure morality to be both the ultimate truth and also devoid of all true reality. It expresses in one and the same breath ideas which it formerly separated. Such a consciousness proclaims by its own actions that it is not serious about this characterization and separation of the moments of the self and inherent reality. On the contrary, it shows that what it announces as absolute existence apart from consciousness, it actually keeps enclosed within the self of self-consciousness; and that what it presents as something entirely in thought, or absolutely inherent and implicit, it treats for that very reason as something which has no truth at all.

It becomes clear to consciousness that placing these moments apart from each other is mentally "*displacing*" them; it is an act of dissemblance, and it would be hypocrisy if it were to really hold to this. But, being pure moral self-consciousness, it flees from this discord between what it represents and what constitutes its essential nature; it flees from this untruth, which presents as true what it holds to be untrue, and, turning away with abhorrence, it hastens back into itself. The consciousness which scorns such a moral idea of the world is pure Conscience (*Gewissen*): it is, in its inmost being, simply spirit consciously assured or "*certain*" (*gewiss*) of itself, spirit which acts directly in the light of this assurance, which acts conscientiously (*gewissenhaft*), without the intervention of those ideas, and finds its true nature in this direct immediacy.

While, however, this sphere of dissemblance is nothing else than the development of moral self-consciousness in its various moments and is consequently its reality, so too this self-consciousness, by returning into itself, will become, in its inmost nature, nothing else. This returning into itself, indeed, simply means that it has come to be conscious that its truth is a pretended truth, a mere pretense. As it returns into itself, it had to be always giving out this pretended truth as its real truth, for it had to express and display itself as an objective idea; but it had to know all the same that this is merely a dissemblance. It would consequently be, in point of fact, hypocrisy all the while, and its abhorrence of such dissemblance would be itself the first expression of hypocrisy.

## CONSCIENCE: THE “BEAUTIFUL SOUL”: EVIL AND

[The one-sidedness of each of the previous stages is removed when the moral consciousness takes on the stance of Conscience. Here the individual is both self-legislating <note>Acting as its own lawmaker</note> and yet certain of the unity and self-completeness of its own will despite the variety of moral choices. The directness involved in the idea of a “self-legislating” will appears in the intuitive clarity of the actions of conscience: it “sees” what is right and does the right without hesitation. But it is not an abstract “faculty” of choosing that is independent of the varied content of the individual’s moral experience. The universality of the individual flows through and fills every part of their being, making them a tangible moral person who is at home with themselves in small details as well as in the larger issues of their self-contained spiritual life. Conscience, as <term>Butler</term> <note>Joseph Butler, an 18th-century philosopher known for his work on ethics and conscience</note> says, is a ‘system’ or ‘constitution,’ similar for the individual to the organized system of the state and its institutions. The self-deception found in the second one-sided phase of moral experience also appears to have no place in Conscience, for Conscience is the clear and self-revealing unity within all the content of moral individuality. Only on this condition can it be absolutely confident and certain of itself in all its functions, and this self-certainty is the essential characteristic of conscience. It believes it cannot be deceived about itself, and can neither mislead itself nor others, but freely achieves everything it claims to be and claims to be everything it achieves. It is thus the highest accomplishment of limited spiritual existence; however, it has no meaning except within the existence of the human spirit in the form of society.]

Its very conditions, however, give rise to delusion and deception of another kind. For its world and its life are so complete that it may attempt to cut itself off from the tangible substance of actual society, which is the only thing that makes the existence of conscience possible. It then tries to develop goodness in lonely isolation from the actual social whole. This is the attitude of the “beautiful soul,” a type of spiritual life developed by the “Moravians” <note>A Protestant denomination known for their focus on personal piety and communal living</note> and made familiar during the Romantic movement. <term>Novalis</term> <note>A pseudonym for Friedrich von Hardenberg, a key figure in German Romanticism</note> is the best-known example; the classical interpretation of the mood was

The consciousness of Absolute Spirit is the attitude of experience known as Religion.]

# CONSCIENCE: THE "BEAUTIFUL SOUL": EVIL AND THE FORGIVENESS OF IT

The antinomy in the moral view of the world—namely, that there is a moral consciousness and yet there is none, or that the validity and obligation of duty have their basis beyond consciousness, and conversely *only* take effect *in* consciousness—these contradictory elements had been combined in the idea where the non-moral consciousness is to pass for moral, its accidental knowledge and will are to be accepted as fully sufficient, and happiness is to be its lot as a matter of grace. Moral self-consciousness did not take this self-contradictory idea upon itself, but transferred it to another being. However, this placing outside itself of what it must think of as necessary is as much a contradiction in form as the other was in content. But that which appears as contradictory, and the division and subsequent resolution of which constitutes the cycle of activity peculiar to the moral attitude, are inherently the same: for pure duty <term>quâ</term> pure knowledge is nothing other than the self of consciousness, and the self of consciousness is existence and reality; and, in the same way, what is supposed to be beyond actual consciousness is nothing other than pure thought—it is, in fact, the self. Because this is so, self-consciousness—for us or <term>per se</term>—returns back into itself and becomes aware that that being is its own self, in which the actual is simultaneously pure knowledge and pure duty.

<summary>This page analyzes the contradictions within the moral worldview, specifically regarding whether duty originates inside or outside of consciousness. It concludes that the self eventually realizes it is the source of both pure knowledge and pure duty, leading self-consciousness to return to itself.</summary>

It considers itself to be absolutely valid in its contingency—as that which knows its own immediate, particular existence as pure knowledge and action, and as the true objective reality and harmony.

This self of Conscience—the phase of spiritual life that is immediately certain of itself as absolute truth and objective being—is the third type of spiritual self. It is the outcome of the third sphere of the spiritual world,<note>That is, Morality; the first being the Ethical Order of Society, and the second being the sphere of cultur<unclear>e</unclear>.</note> and can be briefly contrasted with the two previous types of self.

The totality or actuality revealed as the final result of the ethical world (the world of the social order) is the self of a Person, or ethical personality; its existence lies in being recognized and acknowledged. Since the person is a self devoid of substance, its existence is also an abstract reality. The person has a definite standing, and has it directly and unconditionally; its self is the point within the sphere of its existence that is immediately at rest. That point is not separated from its universality; the two (the particular focus and its universality) are therefore not in a relational process with one another. The universal is present in it without distinction; it is neither the content of the self, nor is the self filled by its own nature.

The second self is the final truth and outcome of a world of culture; it is spirit that has recovered itself after and through disruption, and it is absolute freedom. In this self, the previous immediate unity of individual existence and universality finds its elements separated from one another. Universal will and universal knowledge—the universal is the object and content of the self, and its universal actuality. But the universal does not have there the form of an existence detached from the self; in this mode of self, it therefore receives no filling, no positive content, and no world.

Moral self-consciousness, indeed, allows its universal aspect to become detached, so that this aspect becomes a nature of its own; at the same time, it retains this universality within itself in a superseded form. But it is merely a game of dissembling; it constantly interchanges these two characteristics. In the form of Conscience, with its certainty of itself, it first finds the content to fill the former emptiness of duty as well as the emptiness of right and the empty universal will. And because this certainty of self is also immediate, it finds a definite existence in conscience.

Having reached this level of its truth, moral self-consciousness then leaves—or rather, supersedes—this state of internal division and self-separation, from which arose dissimulation: the separation of its inherent being from the self, of pure duty *as* pure purpose, from reality *as* a nature and a sensory nature opposed to mere purpose. When it has thus returned into itself, it is concrete moral spirit, which does not create for itself a bare abstract standard out of the consciousness of pure duty—a standard to be set up against actual conscious life. On the contrary, pure duty, as well as the sensory nature opposed to pure duty, are superseded moments. This mode of spirit, in its immediate unity, is a moral being making itself actual, and an act is immediately a concrete embodiment of morality.

it in a direct, concrete manner; and at the same time, it *is* merely as conscience knows it to be. When knowledge is something other than its object, it is contingent in character. Spirit, however, which is sure of itself, is not at all an accidental knowledge of that kind; it is not a way of producing ideas within its own being from which reality is divorced. On the contrary; since the separation between what is essential or inherent and the self has been given up, a case of moral action falls—just as it is *per se* <note>in itself</note>—directly within immediate conscious certainty, the sensory [feeling] form of knowledge; and it merely exists *per se* as it is in this form of knowledge.

Action, then, *as* realization, is in this way the pure form of will—the mere conversion of reality (in the sense of a given case) into a reality that is performed and done; the conversion of the mere state of objective knowledge into a state of knowledge about reality as something produced and brought about by consciousness. Just as sensory certainty is directly taken up, or rather converted, into the essential life and substance of spirit, this other transformation is also simple and unmediated—a transition made through pure conception without changing the content, with the content being conditioned by some interest on the part of the consciousness knowing it.

Further, conscience does not break up the circumstances of the case into a variety of duties. It does not operate as the positive general medium in which the various duties, each for itself, would keep their substantial existence undisturbed. If it did so, *either* no action could take place at all, because every concrete case in general contains opposition—and in the specific case of morality, an opposition of duties—and hence there would

It is simple action in accordance with duty—action that does not merely fulfill this or that specific duty, but knows and does what is concretely right. It is, therefore, in general—and for the first time in moral experience—moral action as *action*, and the previous stage of mere consciousness of morality without action has passed into this.

The concrete shape which the act takes may be analyzed by a conscious process of distinction into a variety of properties—*i.e.*, in this case, into a variety of moral relationships. These may either be each expressly held to be absolute (as each must be if it is to be a duty) or, again, subjected to comparison and criticism. In the simple moral action arising from conscience, duties are discarded so indiscriminately that the isolated independence of all these separate entities is immediately destroyed; thus, the process of critically considering and worrying about what our duty is finds no place at all in the unshaken certainty of conscience.

Just as little, again, do we find in conscience that fluctuating uncertainty of mind which first pushes so-called “pure” morality away from itself—assigning it to some other holy being and considering itself unholy—and then, on the other hand, places this moral purity within itself and attributes to that other being the connection of the sensory with the moral element.

The form of moral action is just this very self as a pure process—namely, as the process of knowing—which, in other words, is private individual conviction.
