Duty itself now, *as* duty abandoned by the self, is understood to be merely a phase; it has stopped representing absolute being and has been reduced to something that is not a self, does not exist for its own sake, and is therefore what exists for another. However, this existing-for-another remains an essential phase for that very reason, because the self, *as* consciousness, creates and establishes the opposition between existence-for-self and existence-for-another; and now duty essentially means something immediately real, and is no longer a mere abstract awareness of duty.

This existence for something else is, then, the intrinsically essential substance distinguished from the self. Conscience has not abandoned pure duty, the abstract internal essence: pure duty is the essential phase of relating itself, *as* universality, to others. Conscience is the common element between distinct self-consciousnesses; and this is the substance in which the action secures its stability and reality—the moment that allows recognition by others to take place. 

The moral self-consciousness does not possess this moment of recognition, of pure consciousness which has a definite existence; for that reason, it does not truly “act” at all and does not effectively actualize anything. To it, its own inherent nature is either an abstract, unreal essence or else existence in the form of a reality that has no spiritual character. The actual reality of conscience, however, is one that is a self—that is, an existence conscious of itself, the spiritual element of being recognized. In the same way, the individual fulfills as a duty what other people call violence and wrongdoing—the duty of asserting one’s independence against others; and, again, the duty of preserving one’s life and maintaining the possibility of being useful to one’s neighbors. Others call this cowardice, but what they call courage actually violates both of these duties. But cowardice cannot be so stupid and thoughtless that it does not know that the maintenance of life and the possibility of being useful to others are duties—or so inept as to not be convinced of the dutifulness of its action, and not to know that dutifulness consists in knowledge. Otherwise, it would commit the absurdity of being without morality. Since morality lies in the consciousness of having fulfilled one’s duty, this consciousness will not be lacking when the action is called cowardice any more than when it is called courage. Since the abstraction called "duty" is capable of holding any content, it is perfectly suited to this latter content. The person acting knows what he does to be duty; and since he knows this, and because conviction regarding duty is exactly what dutifulness is, he is thus recognized and acknowledged by others. The act thereby becomes accepted as valid and has actual existence.

It is useless to object to this freedom—which puts one kind of content as well as any other into this universal, inert container of pure duty and pure knowledge—by asserting that another content should have been put there. to affect conscience. The duty it fulfills has a specific content; that content is, undoubtedly, the self of consciousness—its knowledge of itself and its identity with itself. But when fulfilled and placed in the general realm of existence, this identity is no longer just knowledge or the process of making distinctions while simultaneously erasing them. Rather, in the realm of existence, distinction is established as something enduring. The act is a specific, definite one that is not identical to the self-consciousness of everyone else; therefore, it is *not necessarily acknowledged or recognized*. 

Both aspects—conscience *as* (*qua*) acting and the general consciousness that acknowledges the act as duty—remain detached from the specific character of the deed. Because of this freedom and detachment, their relationship within their shared connection is actually one of complete disparity. Consequently, the consciousness that performs and claims the act remains completely uncertain about the spirit that carries it out and is “certain of itself.” This spirit acts and brings a particular, specific quality into existence. Others look to this existence as the truth and find their certainty of the spirit there; in that act, the spirit has expressed what it considers to be its duty. 

However, the spirit is detached and free from any specific duty. It has, therefore, moved beyond the point where others believe it to be. It views the realm of existence and duty as mere passing moments. What it places before them, it also “displaces” again—or rather, by that very fact (*eo ipso*), it has immediately “displaced” it. For, to the spirit, its reality is not the duty or the specific content thus

put forward, but rather is the reality it possesses in its absolute certainty of itself.

Other self-consciousnesses do not know, then, whether this particular conscience is morally good or wicked; or, rather, they not only cannot know this conscience, but they must also assume it to be wicked. For just as it stands detached from the specific content of duty and is disconnected from duty as an inherent existence, they do the same. They themselves know how to "displace" or disguise what is placed before them: it is something that expresses merely the self of another individual, not their own. They do not only know themselves to be detached and free from it, but they must also dissolve and dissipate it within their own consciousness, reducing it to nothingness through judgments and explanations in order to preserve their own self.

But the act of conscience is not merely this determination of existence—a specific content abandoned by the pure self. What should be binding as duty and recognized as such is only so through the knowledge and conviction that it *is* duty, by the self's knowledge of itself in the performed deed. When the deed ceases to contain this element of self, it ceases to be what is its own essential nature. If its existence were deserted by this consciousness of self, it would be an ordinary reality, and the act would appear to us as a way of fulfilling one’s own pleasure and desire. What ought to exist has essentiality here only because it is known to be individuality expressing itself. And this being known is the fact acknowledged and recognized by others, and is that which, as such, ought to exist.

The self enters existence as self. The spirit that is certain of itself exists as such for others; its immediate

# Conscience

The act is not what is accepted and real; what is acknowledged by others is not the determinate element, nor the inherent being, but solely and simply the self knowing itself as such. The element which gives permanence and stability is universal self-consciousness. What enters this element cannot be the effect of the act: the latter does not last there and maintains no permanence; only self-consciousness is what is recognized and gains concrete reality.

Here again,<note>See page 512 and following.</note> then, we see Language to be the form in which spirit finds existence. Language is the way self-consciousness exists for *others*; it is self-consciousness which is immediately present there as such, and in the form of this actual universal self-consciousness. Language is the self separating itself from itself, which comes objectively before itself as the pure ego identical with the ego, which at once maintains itself in this objective form as *this* actual self, and at the same time fuses directly with others and is *their* self-consciousness. The self perceives itself at the same time that it is perceived by others; and this perceiving is just existence which has become a self.

The content which language has here obtained is no longer the self we found in the world of culture—perverted, perverting, and distraught. It is spirit which, having returned to itself, is certain of itself, certain in itself of its truth, of its own act of recognition, and of being recognized as *this* knowledge. The language of the ethical spirit of society is law, and simple command and complaint, which is only a tear shed over necessity. Moral consciousness, on the other hand, remains silent, shut up within its inner life; for the self has no existence

...as yet in its case; rather, existence and the self stand there, in the first instance, in an external relationship to each other. Language, however, emerges merely as the mediating element between independent self-consciousnesses that are recognized and acknowledged; and the existing self means immediate universal recognition—it means recognition in many ways, and within this very manifoldness, simple recognition. What the language of conscience contains is the self knowing itself as an essential reality. This alone is what that language expresses, and this expression is the true realization of "doing" anything, and renders the act valid and acceptable. Consciousness expresses its conviction: in this conviction alone is the action a duty; it counts as duty, too, solely because the conviction is expressed. For universal self-consciousness stands detached from the specific act which merely exists; the act *as* existence means nothing to it. What it considers important is the conviction that the act is a duty, and this appears concretely in language.

To realize the act here does not mean translating its content from the form of purpose, or subjectivity, into the form of abstract reality; it means translating it from the form of immediate self-certainty—which takes its knowledge and its self-existence to be the essential fact—into the form of the assurance that consciousness is convinced of its duty and, as conscience, knows for itself what duty is. This assurance thus guarantees that it is convinced that its conviction is the essential fact.

In the willing of the self that is certain of itself—in this knowledge of the self as the essential reality—lies the essence of what is right.

Therefore, when anyone says they are acting from conscience, they are telling the truth, because their conscience is the self that knows and wills. So far as this sphere of conscience still distinguishes its abstract consciousness from its self-consciousness, its life is merely hidden in God. God is indeed immediately present to its mind and heart—to its very self. But what is revealed—its actual consciousness and the mediating process of this consciousness—is, to it, something other than that hidden inner life and the immediacy of God's presence. However, with the completion of conscience, the distinction between its abstract consciousness and its self-consciousness is abolished. It knows that the abstract consciousness is simply this self—this individual self-existence which is certain of itself. It knows that the very difference between these terms is removed in the immediacy of the relation of the self to the ultimate Being. When that Being is placed outside the self, it is merely an abstract essence and a Being concealed from it. For a relation is mediated when the terms related are not one and the same, but each is a different term for the other, and they are joined as one only through some third term. An immediate relation, however, means, in fact, nothing other than the unity of the terms. It may well preserve itself in its purity, for it does not act; it is hypocrisy, which wants to see the act of judging taken for the actual deed, and instead of proving its integrity and honesty by acts, it does so by expressing fine sentiments. It is thus constituted in exactly the same way as that which it reproaches for putting phrases in the place of duty. In both cases alike, the aspect of reality is distinct from the express statements—in the one case owing to the selfish purpose of the action, and in the other through the failure to act at all, a result which is inevitable when there is mere talk about duty; for duty without deeds is altogether meaningless.

The act of judging, however, has also to be looked at as a positive act of thought and has a positive content: this aspect makes the contradiction present in the apprehending consciousness, and its identity with the first consciousness, still more complete. The active consciousness declares its specific deed to be its duty, and the consciousness that passes judgment cannot deny

It focuses on the other aspect instead, redirecting the act into the inner realm and explaining the act through selfish motives and inner intentions—intentions that differ from the act itself. Just as every act can be treated in terms of its dutifulness, each can also be considered from this other point of view of particularity; for as an act, it is the actualization of an individual.

This process of judging, then, removes the act from the sphere of its objective existence and turns it back toward the inner realm, into the form of specific and individual particularity. If the act brings glory with it, then the inner aspect is judged as a desire for fame. If it fits perfectly with the position and status of the individual without exceeding it—and is structured so that the individual does not treat their position as an external appendage, but provides the content for this universality through themselves, proving they are capable of a higher status—then the inner nature of the act is judged as ambition, and so on. No hero is a hero to his valet; not, however, because the hero is not a hero, but because the valet is—the valet, with whom the hero has to deal, not as a hero, but as a man who eats, drinks, and dresses; who, in short, appears as a specific individual with certain personal needs and quirks. In the same way, there is no act in which that process of judgment cannot oppose the particular aspect of individuality to the universal aspect of the act, and set the valet of morality against the hero who performs the act.<note>* Compare with the *Philosophy of History*, Introduction (English translation, page 32 and following).</note>

The consciousness that passes judgment in this way is, consequently, *itself* base and mean, because it breaks the act apart and brings out and holds onto its inherent inconsistency and inner conflict. It is, furthermore, hypocrisy, because it presents this way of judging not as another form of being wicked, but as the correct understanding of the act. It sets itself up, in its unreality—in this vanity of knowing well and knowing better—far above the deeds it criticizes, and it wants its mere words without deeds to be accepted as an admirable kind of reality.

They exist *for each other*, these absolutely opposed elements; it is the completely inner reality that has, in this way, come into opposition with itself and entered objective existence. They constitute pure knowledge, which, because of this opposition, takes the form of consciousness. But so far, it is not yet *self-consciousness*. It achieves this realization through the process that this opposition undergoes. For this opposition is really the undivided continuity and identity of ego = ego; and each side, by itself, inherently cancels itself out through the contradiction in its pure universality. While this universality implies continuity and identity, it simultaneously resists its identity with the other and separates itself from it. Through this surrender of separate selfhood, the knowledge—which in its existence is in a state of <term>diremption</term> <note>a forceful division or separation of a unity into two</note>—returns into the unity of the self. It is the concrete, actual Ego: a universal knowledge of the self within its absolute opposite. This is found in the knowledge that is internal to and within the self, which—because of the very purity of its separate subjective existence—is itself completely universal. The reconciling affirmation, the "yes," by which both egos cease their existence in opposition, is the existence of the ego expanded into a duality—an ego that remains one and identical with itself within that duality, and possesses the certainty of itself in its complete surrender and its opposite. It is God appearing among those who know themselves in the form of pure knowledge.

<page-num>683</page-num>
<header>### (CC) RELIGION</header>

The appearance of Absolute Spirit as a principle that constitutes a distinctive stage of experience on its own is both a requirement of the preceding development and a condition for making experience complete. Finite or socialized spiritual existence is, at its best, unable to establish the truth that "Spirit is the only reality." This is because the more finite spirit approaches the state of claiming to be self-contained, the more it depends on universal self-consciousness. An Absolute Spiritual Being—one that is trans-finite—is therefore necessary to realize and sustain the full meaning that finite spirit possesses. Moreover, if "the truth is the whole," and truth is only self-complete and self-explaining in that way—and if reality is essentially spiritual—then experience only finds its complete meaning realized in the principle of Absolute Spirit. Therefore, the final stage of the *Phenomenology* of experience is the appearance of Absolute Spirit within it.

Furthermore, Absolute Spirit, in its own distinctive existence, could only appear at the end of the process of experience. The entire process is required to reveal and create the substance that makes up the Absolute. But the unique feature of the stage now reached is that here the Absolute operates in its undivided totality to form a specific type of experience; or, in the language of the text, we have the Absolute here "conscious of itself." No doubt, in all the previous stages—"consciousness," "self-consciousness," "reason," and "spirit"—the Absolute has been implied as a limiting principle, both supporting and defining the boundaries of each stage. Consequently, each stage had an Absolute of its own, the character of which was derived in each case from the specific features of that stage. Now, however, we have the Absolute by itself, in its single self-completeness, as the sole forming factor of a specific type of experience.

The Absolute, then, in its own self-complete reality, appears as the foundational principle of experience. Experience here is the self-consciousness of Absolute Spirit; it appears to itself in all its objects. Since all the modes of finitude considered so far (consciousness, self-consciousness, etc.) are embraced within its single totality, it may use any and all of these various modes as the media through which to appear.

When it appears in and through these modes of finitude, we have the attitude of Religion. Since these modes, as we saw, differ, the religious attitude differs; and accordingly, we have various types or forms of religion.

Each of these forms, in and through which the Absolute appears, is limited in its nature and process; each is *in itself* inadequate to reveal complete absolute self-consciousness. Hence, the variety of religions is necessitated by and is indirectly due to the failure of any one type, and the inadequacy of every single type, to reveal the Absolute completely. A form of appearance or self-manifestation of the Absolute is therefore required which will reveal Absolute Spirit adequately to itself as it essentially is in itself. Here it will know itself, so to speak, face to face, and with perfect completeness. This form is *Absolute Knowledge*. Hence, Religion and Absolute Knowledge are the final stages in the argument of the *Phenomenology*. The former is dealt with in the immediately following section (VII) and its various subsections; the latter forms the subject of the concluding section (VIII) of the work.]

# VII

## RELIGION IN GENERAL

IN the forms of experience previously discussed—which are distinguished broadly as Consciousness, Self-consciousness, Reason, and Spirit—Religion, the consciousness of Absolute Being in general, has certainly already appeared. But that was from the perspective of consciousness when it treats the Absolute Being as its object. Absolute Being, however, in its own distinctive nature—the Self-consciousness of Spirit—has not appeared in those forms.

Even at the level of Consciousness, namely when it takes the form of "Understanding," there is a consciousness of the <term>supersensible</term>, of the inner being of objective existence. But the supersensible, the eternal, or whatever we choose to call it, lacks selfhood. To begin with, it is merely something universal, which is still a long way from being spirit knowing itself as spirit.

Then there was Self-consciousness, which reached its final form in the "bereft soul," the "unhappy consciousness"; that was merely the pain and sorrow of spirit struggling to project itself into objectivity once more, but not succeeding. The unity of individual self-consciousness with its unchangeable Being—which is what this stage arrives at—remains, consequently, a "beyond," something far off.

<summary>This page introduces the transition to the study of religion, noting that while the concept of Absolute Being appeared in earlier stages of consciousness, it has not yet been realized as the self-consciousness of Spirit. It reviews how previous stages like Understanding and the Unhappy Consciousness perceived the divine as either a characterless universal or an unreachable "beyond."</summary>
<keywords>Religion, Absolute Being, Consciousness, Self-consciousness, Understanding, supersensible, Unhappy Consciousness, Spirit, objectivity</keywords>

--- Page 272 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of how religion emerges from different stages of spirit, specifically moving from the state of Reason and the Ethical Order toward a more developed consciousness of Absolute Being.</meta>

Phenomenology of Mind

The immediate existence of Reason (which we found arising out of that state of sorrow) and the special shapes which reason assumes have no form of religion, because self-consciousness, in the case of reason, knows itself or looks for itself in the direct and immediate present.

On the other hand, in the world of the Ethical Order, we met with a type of religion: the religion of the netherworld. This is a belief in the fearful and unknown darkness of Fate, and in the Eumenides of the spirit of the departed. The former is pure negation taking the form of universality; the latter is the same negation but in the form of particularity. Absolute Being is, then, in this latter shape, undoubtedly the self and is present, as there is no other way for the self to *be* except as present. But the particular self is this specific ghostly shade, which keeps the universal element, Fate, separated from itself. It is indeed a shade, a ghost, a canceled and superseded particular, and so a universal self. But that negative meaning has not yet turned around into this latter positive significance; hence the self, so canceled and transcended, still directly means at the same time this particular being, this insubstantial reality. Fate, however, without the self, remains the darkness of night devoid of consciousness, which never comes to draw distinctions within itself and never attains the clarity of self-knowledge.

This belief in a necessity that produces nothingness—this belief in the netherworld—becomes a belief in Heaven, because the self which has departed must be united with its universal nature; it must unfold what it contains in terms of this universality, and thus

become clear to itself. This kingdom of belief, however, we saw reveal its content merely in the element of reflective thought (*Denken*), without bringing out the true concept (*Begriff*); and we saw it, for that reason, perish in its final fate, namely in the religion of enlightenment. Here in this type of religion, the supersensible "beyond," which we found in "understanding," is reinstated again. However, it is restored in such a way that self-consciousness rests and feels satisfied in the mundane present, not in the "beyond." It thinks of the supersensible beyond as void and empty, unknowable, and free of all terrors—perceiving it neither as a "self" nor as a force of power and might.

In the religion of Morality, it is finally established that Absolute Reality has a positive content; but that content is bound up with the negativity characteristic of the enlightenment. The content is an objective being, which is at the same time taken back into the self and remains enclosed there. It is a content with internal distinctions, while its parts are just as immediately negated as they are established. The final destiny, however, which absorbs this contradictory process, is the self-conscious of itself as the controlling necessity (*Schicksal*) of what is essential and actual.

Spirit knowing itself is, in religion, primarily and immediately its own pure self-consciousness. Those modes of it considered above—"objective spirit," "spirit alienated from itself," and "spirit certain of itself"—together constitute what spirit is in its condition of consciousness. This is the state in which, being objectively opposed to its own world, it does not yet grasp and consciously possess itself within it. But in Conscience, it brings itself, as well as its objective world as a whole,

# A

## NATURAL RELIGION

[The arrangement of the analysis of religion and its division into various subsections are—as indicated in the preceding note (p. 683)—determined by the general development of experience. That development moves from the immediate through mediation to the fusion of immediacy and mediation. The stages of the development of experience are Consciousness, Self-consciousness, and Reason, with Reason leading to its highest level—finite spiritual existence. The development of religion follows these various ways in which objects are presented in experience, and the three primary divisions of religion are determined accordingly: Natural Religion is religion at the level of Consciousness; Art is religion at the level of Self-consciousness; and Revealed Religion is religion at the level of Reason and Spirit. Each of these is subdivided again, and the subdivisions follow more or less closely the various levels of these three fundamental stages of experience—Consciousness, etc. Thus, in Natural Religion, we have religion at the level of sense-certainty (*“Light”*), religion at the level of perception (*“Life”*), and religion at the level of understanding—where the reciprocal relationship formed by the *“play of forces”* appears as the relationship of the *“Artificer”* to his own product.

This general principle is not worked out in the same obvious detail for the other two primary types of religion—Art and Revealed Religion. However, the same general method of development is followed in those cases as well.

The historical material the writer considers consists, as might be expected, of the various religions that have appeared throughout human history. However, these religions are treated as illustrations of the principles dominating the religious consciousness in general, rather than as merely historical phenomena.

The following argument should be read alongside Hegel’s *Philosophy of Religion*, Part II, Sections I and II, and Part III.]

# NATURAL RELIGION

Spirit knowing spirit is the consciousness of itself; it exists for itself in the form of objectivity. It exists, and is at the same time self-existent (*Fürsichsein*). It exists for itself; this is the aspect of self-consciousness, and it exists in contrast to the aspect of its consciousness—the aspect through which it relates to itself as an object. Within its consciousness, there is an opposition and, consequently, a specific character to the form in which it appears to itself and knows itself. In considering religion, we are concerned only with this specific character, because its essential, unspecified principle—its abstract notion—has already been revealed. However, the distinction between consciousness and self-consciousness also falls within this concept. The form or shape of religion does not view the existence of spirit as nature detached and free from thought, nor as thought detached from existence. Instead, the shape assumed by religion is existence held and preserved within thought, as well as a thought-content that exists consciously.

One religion is distinguished from another by the specific character of this form in which the spirit knows itself. At the same time, we must note that the systematic explanation of this self-knowledge, in terms of this particular specific character, does not actually exhaust the whole—

Its goal is to give the form of self-consciousness to the specific shape that serves as the object of consciousness. This distinction, however, is not *by that very fact* transcended simply because the shapes contained within that consciousness also possess an element of the "self," or because God is represented as self-consciousness. The self as it is consciously presented is not the actual, concrete self. Additionally, the lower determination must show itself to be canceled, transcended, and understood by the higher one. For what is merely "represented" (*Vorgestellt*) only stops being something "represented" and alien or external to its own knowledge when the self has produced it. In doing so, the self views the characteristics of the object as its own characteristics, thereby seeing itself in that object. Through this operation, the lower determination <note>that of being something “represented”</note> immediately vanishes; for every action is a negative process carried out at the expense of something else. It is not appropriate here to return from the total sum of specific determinations back to a single determination and show how the fullness of all the others is contained within it and its particular form of religion. When a higher form is placed under a lower one, it is stripped of its significance for the self-conscious spirit; it belongs to the spirit only superficially and exists for it only at the level of a representation <note>Hegel's *Vorstellung*</note>. The higher form must be considered in its own unique significance and addressed where it serves as the principle of a specific religion, validated and approved by its actual spirit.

### a

## GOD AS LIGHT <note>This refers to the Parsee religion, or Zoroastrianism.</note>

<term>Spirit</term>, as the <term>Absolute Being</term> that is <term>self-consciousness</term>—or the self-conscious Absolute Being that is all truth and knows all reality as itself—is, at first, merely its own <term>concept</term> and principle. This stands in contrast to the reality it gains through the process of its conscious activity. Compared to the clear daylight of that fully realized development, this <term>concept</term> is the darkness and night of its inner life. Unlike the existence of its various stages as independent forms and shapes, this <term>concept</term> is the creative secret of its birth. This secret contains its own revelation; for existence has a necessary place in this <term>concept</term>, because the <term>concept</term> is spirit knowing itself, and thus naturally possesses the capacity to be conscious and to present itself objectively. Here we have the <term>pure ego</term> which, by externalizing itself and seeing itself as a universal object, possesses self-certainty. In other words, for the ego, this object is the fusion of all thought and all reality.

When the first and immediate division occurs within self-knowing <term>Absolute Spirit</term>, its form takes on the character of immediate consciousness or <term>sense-certainty</term>. It perceives itself in the form of *being*; yet not *being* in the sense of what is without...

Because of this characteristic, this mode is the pure, all-containing, all-suffusing Light of the East, which preserves itself in its formless, indeterminate substantiality. Its counterpart, its otherness, is the equally simple negative—Darkness. But the essential simplicity of its thought rambles and roves about, inconstant and inconsistent; it enlarges its boundaries to a measureless extent, and its beauty, heightened to splendor, is lost in its sublimity.<note>Compare *Philosophy of Religion*, W.W., XI, 403, 404, 411.</note>

### PLANTS AND ANIMALS AS OBJECTS OF RELIGION<note>Primarily religions of India.</note>

Self-conscious spirit, passing away from abstract, formless Essence and going into itself—or, in other words, having raised its immediacy to the level of the Self—makes its simple unity assume the character of a multitude of self-existing entities; this is the Religion of spiritual Sense-Perception. Here, spirit breaks up into an innumerable plurality of weaker and stronger, richer and poorer spirits. This Pantheism, which to begin with consists in the quiet stability of these spiritual atoms, passes into a process of active internal hostility. The innocence that characterizes the flower and plant religions, and which is merely the selfless idea of the Self, gives way to the seriousness of struggling, warring life—to the guilt of animal religions. The stillness and helplessness of merely contemplative individuality pass into the destructive violence of separate self-existence.

It is of no use to have removed the lifelessness of abstraction from the things of perception and to have raised them to the level of realities of spiritual perception: the life of this spiritual kingdom has death at its heart, owing to the fact of <term>determinateness</term> and the inherent negativity that invades and encroaches upon their innocent and harmless indifference toward one another. These spirits fight and hate each other to the death and consciously accept specific animal forms as their essential reality and their god<note>Sacred animals in Indian religion.</note>: for they are nothing more than animal spirits—animal lives separated and cut off from one another, with no sense of universality consciously present within them.

However, the characteristic of purely negative, independent existence consumes itself in this active hatred toward one another. Through this process, which is inherent in its very principle, spirit enters into another form. This cancelled and abolished independent existence takes the form of the object—a form produced by the self, or rather, it is the self produced: the self-consuming self, which is to say, the self that becomes a "thing." Therefore, the active agent maintains control over these animal spirits that are merely tearing each other to pieces; his action is not merely negative, but stable and creative. Thus, the consciousness of spirit is now the process that exists above and beyond its immediate, inherent [universal] nature, and it also transcends abstract, isolated existence. ## THE ARTIFICER <note>Egyptian religions.</note>

Spirit, then, here takes the form of the artificer, and its action—when producing itself as an object without yet having grasped the thought of itself—is an instinctive kind of work, like bees building their cells.

The first form, because it is immediate, has the abstract character of "understanding," and the work accomplished is not yet in itself filled with spirit. The crystals of Pyramids and Obelisks—simple combinations of straight lines with flat surfaces and equal relations of parts in which the incommensurability of curvature is set aside—these are the works produced in strict geometrical form by this artificer. Due to the purely abstract, intellectual nature of the form, it is not in itself the true significance of the form; it is not the spiritual self. Thus, either the works produced only receive spirit into them as an alien, departed spirit—one that has abandoned its living infusion and permeation of reality and, being dead itself, enters into these lifeless crystals; or they assume an external relation to spirit as something which is itself external and not present as spirit—they are related to it as they are to the rising Light, which casts its significance upon them.

Through his work, he has raised himself to the point where his conscious life breaks apart, where spirit greets spirit. These monsters in form and shape, word and deed, are resolved and dissolved into a shape which is spiritual—an outer form which has entered into itself, and an inner essence which expresses itself out of itself and in itself. They pass into thought, which brings forth itself, preserves the shape and form suited to thought, and is a transparent existence. Spirit is an *Artist.*

# B

## RELIGION IN THE FORM OF ART <note>Greek religion.</note>

Spirit has elevated the shape in which it is an object for its own consciousness into the form of consciousness itself, and spirit places such a form before itself. The craftsman has abandoned that external activity of synthesis—that blending of the different forms of thought and nature. Once the shape has acquired the form of self-conscious activity, the craftsman has become a spiritual worker.

If we then ask what the actual spirit is that finds the consciousness of its Absolute in the religion of art, it turns out to be the ethical or objective spirit. This spirit is not just the universal substance of all individuals; rather, when this substance is said to possess the form of consciousness as an objective fact for actual consciousness, it means that the substance—which is individualized—is recognized by the individuals within it as their own essence and their own accomplishment. For them, it is neither the "Light of the World" (in whose unity the self-existence of self-consciousness is held only negatively and fleetingly, and which beholds a lord and master of its reality), nor is it the restless waste and destruction of hostile nations, nor their subjection to "castes," which together create only the appearance of organization.

<summary>This page defines the "religion of art" as the stage where spirit moves from blending natural and thought forms to creating self-conscious, ethical expressions of its own essence. This ethical spirit is recognized by individuals as their own achievement and identity rather than a foreign or destructive master.</summary>
<keywords>Spirit, religion of art, ethical spirit, objective spirit, self-consciousness, craftsman, Greek religion, castes</keywords>

of a completed whole where, however, the universal freedom of the individuals involved is lacking. Instead, this spirit is a free nation in which custom and order form the common substance of everyone; each person knows that the reality and existence of this substance is their own will and their own action.

The religion of the ethical spirit, however, elevates it above its actual realization and represents a return from its objectivity into pure knowledge of itself. Since a nation built on ethics lives in direct unity with its own substance and does not yet contain the principle of pure individual self-consciousness, the religion characteristic of this sphere only appears in its complete form when that stable security is broken. For the reality of the ethical substance depends partly on its quiet unchangeableness, in contrast to the absolute process of self-consciousness. Consequently, it depends on the fact that this self-consciousness has not yet left its peaceful life of tradition and its confident security within it to look inward. Furthermore, that reality rests on its organization into a variety of rights and duties, as well as its organized distribution into different social roles and classes. Each group has its specific way of acting that contributes to the whole. Therefore, it relies on the fact that the individual is satisfied with the limits of their existence and has not yet grasped the unrestricted thought of their own free self. But that peaceful, immediate confidence in the substance of this ethical life eventually returns to a trust and certainty in the self. The plurality of rights and duties, along with the limited, specific actions they involve, undergoes the same <term>dialectic process</term> in the realm of ethical life as the plurality of “things” does in other spheres.

The complete fulfillment of the ethical life within free self-consciousness, and the destined consummation (*Schicksal* <note>Fate or destiny</note>) of the ethical world, are therefore found when individuality has entered into itself. This condition is one of absolute lightness on the part of the ethical spirit; it has dissipated and dissolved into itself all the firmly established distinctions that constitute its own stability, as well as the separate components of its own structured organization. Being perfectly sure of itself, it has attained a boundless cheerfulness of heart and the freest enjoyment of itself. This simple certainty of spirit within itself has a double meaning: it is quiet stability and solid truth, as well as absolute unrest and the disappearance of the ethical order. It turns, however, toward the latter; for the truth of the ethical spirit lies primarily in this substantial objectivity and trust, in which the self does not think of itself as a free individual. Consequently, in this inner subjectivity, by becoming a free self, the ethical spirit collapses. Since its trust is then broken and the substance of the nation is fractured, the spirit—which was the connecting medium of the unstable extremes—has now emerged as an extreme: that of self-consciousness taking itself to be essential and ultimate. This is the spirit certain within itself, which mourns the loss of its world and now produces its own essential being out of the abstraction of the self, raised far above actual reality.

Spirit acts in this individual as his universal essence and his power, from which he suffers violence, acting as his element of "<term>Pathos</term>."

## THE ABSTRACT WORK OF ART

The first work of art is abstract and particular because it is immediate. From its own side, it must move away from this immediate and objective phase toward self-consciousness. On the other side, self-consciousness strives within the "cult" to eliminate the distinction it initially established in contrast to its own spirit; by doing so, it aims to produce a work of art that is inherently endowed with life.

The first way the artistic spirit keeps its form and its active consciousness as far apart as possible is immediate in character—the assumed form exists simply as a "thing" in general. It breaks down into the distinction of particularity, which contains the form of the self, and universality, which represents the inorganic elements relative to the adopted form, serving as its environment and habitation. This assumed shape obtains its pure form—the form belonging to spirit—by the whole being raised into the sphere of the pure concept. It is not like the crystal, which we saw belongs to the level of understanding—a form that housed and covered a lifeless element or was illuminated externally by a soul. Nor, again, is it that mixing of the forms of nature and thought which first appeared in connection with plants, where the activity of thought was still merely an imitation. Rather, the concept strips off

The simplicity of this form has abolished all this individuation and brought it together into an individuality at peace with itself. # The Abstract Work of Art

The content of this unique and individual form of speech is provided by the general, determinate character that the Absolute Spirit adopts within its religion. Thus, the universal spirit of the East, which has not yet particularized its existence, utters equally simple, abstract, and universal statements about the Absolute. The substantial content of these statements is sublime in its simple truth; however, because of this universality, it simultaneously appears trivial to a more developed self-consciousness.

The more developed self, which advances toward existing distinctively *for itself*, rises above the pure “pathos” of <note>unconscious</note> substance. It gains mastery over the objectivity of the principle of Light found in Eastern religion and recognizes that the simplicity of abstract truth is the inherent reality (*das Ansichseyende*). This reality does not take the form of a contingent existence through the speech of an alien self, but is the certain and unwritten law of the gods—a law that “lives forever, and no one knows when it first appeared.”

Just as the universal truth revealed by the “Light” of the world has now returned to what is inward or what lies beneath, and has thus shed the form of contingent appearance; so too, on the other hand, in the religion of art—because God’s form has taken on consciousness and therefore general particularity—the unique utterance of God, who is the spirit of an ethically organized nation, is the Oracle. The Oracle knows the nation's specific circumstances and situation and announces what is beneficial to its interests. Reflective thought, however, is satisfied by the universal truths stated, because these are known as the essential, implicit reality of the nation’s life.

For what is accidental is something undiscerned, undiscriminated, and extraneous; and hence, the ethical consciousness allows itself—as if by a throw of the dice—to settle the matter in a manner that is similarly undiscriminating and extraneous. If an individual, through his understanding, decides on a certain course and selects, after consideration, what is useful for him, it is the specific nature of his particular character that is the ground of this self-determination. This basis is precisely what is contingent; and the knowledge that his understanding provides regarding what is useful for the individual is, therefore, just the same kind of knowledge as that of “oracles” or the “lot.” The only difference is that he who questions the oracle or the lot thereby shows the ethical sentiment of indifference to what is accidental, while the former, on the contrary, treats the inherently contingent as an essential concern of his thought and knowledge. The true self-conscious existence that spirit receives in the form of speech—which is not the utterance of an external and therefore accidental (meaning non-universal) self-consciousness—is the work of art we encountered previously. It stands in contrast to the statue, which has the character of a “thing.” Just as the statue represents existence in a state of rest, the other represents existence in a state of transience. In the case of the statue, objectivity is set free and does away with the immediate presence of the actual self; in the latter, however, objectivity is too closely bound to the self, fails to reach a definite physical form, and, like time, is gone as soon as it appears.

The religious <term>Cult</term> constitutes the process of these two sides—a process in which the divine embodiment moving within the pure feeling of self-consciousness, and its embodiment at rest in the form of <term>thinghood</term>, mutually abandon their distinct characters. Consequently, the unity that is the underlying principle of their being becomes an existing fact. Here in the Cult, the self gains a consciousness of the <term>Divine Being</term> descending from its remoteness into it; this Divine Being, which was previously unreal and merely objective, thereby receives the true reality of self-consciousness.

The purity it thus attains is immediately and only <term>absolute Being</term>, and it is one with absolute Being. This <term>ceremonial cult</term>, in its first form, exists only in secret; that is, it is merely a performance accomplished subjectively in thought and is unrealized. It must become a real act, for an "unreal act" is a contradiction in terms. Through this, actual consciousness rises to the level of its pure <term>self-consciousness</term>. The <term>essential Being</term> has the significance of a free object within it; through the actual cult, this object returns to the self. Insofar as it has the significance of absolute Being dwelling in its purity beyond actual reality in pure consciousness, this Being descends—through this mediating process of the cult—from its <term>universality</term> into an individual form, and thus combines and unites with actual reality.

<header>THE LIVING WORK OF ART</header>

The nation that approaches its god through the cult of the religion of art is an ethically organized nation, knowing its State and the actions of the State to be the will and the achievement of its own activity. This universal spirit, confronting the self-conscious nation, is consequently not the “Light” of the world—which, being selfless, does not contain the certainty of individual selves, but is only their universal ultimate Being and the dominating, commanding power in which they disappear. The religious cult of this simple, un-embodied ultimate Being therefore gives back to its followers mainly just this: that they are the nation of their god. It secures for them only their stable existence and their bare substance as a whole; it does not secure for them their actual self; this is indeed rejected. For they revere their god as an empty, profound depth, not as spirit.

The cult of the religion of art, on the other hand, does away with 그 abstract simplicity of the absolute Being, and therefore with its “profundity.” But that Being, which is directly at one with the self, is inherently spirit and comprehending truth, although it is not yet known explicitly—in other words, it does not yet know the “depths” of its own nature. Because this Absolute, then, implies a self, consciousness finds itself at home with it.

In being useful for food and drink, it reaches its highest perfection. For in this, there is the possibility of a higher existence, and it comes in contact with spiritual existence. In its metamorphosis, the spirit of the earth has developed and become partly a silently energizing substance and partly a spiritual ferment; in the first case, it is the feminine principle, the nursing mother; in the other, it is the masculine principle, the self-driving force of self-conscious existence.

In this enjoyment, then, that Orient <note>The "Light" of the world, as defined previously.</note> “Light” of the world is discovered for what it really is: enjoyment is the mystery of its being. For mysticism is not the concealment of a secret, or ignorance; it consists in the self knowing itself to be one with absolute Being, and in this latter, therefore, becoming revealed. Only the self is revealed to itself; or, what is manifest is so merely in the immediate certainty of itself. But it is precisely in such certainty that simple absolute Being has been placed by the cult. As a thing that can be used, it does not only have an existence that is seen, felt, smelled, or tasted; it is also an object of desire, and, by actually being enjoyed, it becomes one with the self, and is thereby completely disclosed to this self and made manifest.

When we say of anything, “it is manifest to reason, to the heart,” it is, in point of fact, still a secret; for it still lacks the actual certainty of immediate existence—both the certainty regarding what is objective and the certainty of enjoyment. In religion, however, this is not only an immediate and unreflecting certainty, but at the same time a fully cognitive certainty of the self.

## THE SPIRITUAL WORK OF ART

The national spirits, which find their existence in the form of some particular animal, merge into one single spirit.* Thus, the separate, artistically beautiful national spirits combine to form a Pantheon, whose element and habitation is Language. When the national or tribal spirit is realized, the pure intuition of the self—in the sense of universal human nature—takes this form: the national spirit joins with others (which, together with it, constitute one people through nature and natural conditions) in a common undertaking. For this task, it builds up a collective nation and, along with it, a collective heaven. This universality, which spirit achieves in its existence, is nevertheless merely the first stage of universality. To begin with, it starts from the individuality of ethical life, has not yet overcome its immediate nature, and has not yet built a single state out of these separate national elements. The ethical life of an actual national spirit rests partly on the simple, confiding trust that individuals have in the whole of their nation, and partly on the direct share that everyone—despite differences in status—takes in the decisions and actions of its government. There are two sides to the business that the universal activity aims to accomplish: the side of the self—by which it is brought about by a collection of actual nations led by prominent individuals; and the side of the universal—by which it is brought about by their fundamental forces. However, the relationship between these two previously took on the character of a synthetic connection between the universal and the individual—that is, the process of ideal representation. The judgment regarding this world depends on this specific character.

By this means, the relationship between the two is a blending of both, which illogically divides the unity of the action and unnecessarily shifts the act from one side to the other. The universal powers take on the form of individual beings and thus possess within themselves the principle from which action originates; therefore, when they achieve anything, it seems to proceed entirely from them and to be as free as human action. Consequently, both gods and men have performed one and the same deed. The seriousness with which those divine powers set to work is ridiculously unnecessary, since they are, in fact, the moving force behind the individuals engaged in the acts. Meanwhile, the strain and toil of the individuals is an equally useless effort, since the divine powers direct and manage everything. Over-zealous mortal creatures, who are as nothing, are at the same time the mighty self that subdues universal beings, violates the gods, and provides them with actual reality and an interest in acting. Just as the gods fall into this contradictory relationship with the opposing nature that takes the form of the self, their universality similarly comes into conflict with their own specific character and the relationship it has with others. The specific character they possess is rooted in divine subsistence and, despite its specific limitations, possesses the independence of a complete individuality. Because of this, their characters immediately lose the sharpness of their distinct peculiarities and blend together in their ambiguity.

It is conscious of an equally helpless pity and, finally, the mere empty peace of surrendering to necessity, whose work is understood neither as the necessary act of character nor as the action of the <term>absolute Being</term> within itself.

The ethical substance becomes divided in its form—that is, with respect to knowledge. When <term>Spirit</term> acts, it appears as consciousness in opposition to the object toward which its activity is directed; consequently, that object is defined as the negative of the knowing agent. In this way, the agent finds himself in the conflict between knowing and not knowing. He derives his purpose from his own character and recognizes it as an essential ethical fact. However, because of the specific nature of his character, he only recognizes one power of the substance; the other remains hidden and out of sight from him. Therefore, objectively present reality is one thing in itself and something else for consciousness. 

In this context, the higher and lower rights come to signify the power that knows and reveals itself to consciousness, and the power that conceals itself and lurks in the background. The first is the aspect of light, the god of the Oracle, who in his natural aspect (as Light) has sprung from the all-illuminating Sun. He knows all and reveals all—Phoebus and his father, Zeus. But the commands of this truth-speaking god, and his proclamations of what *is*, are actually deceptive and misleading. For this knowledge is, by its very principle, fundamentally *not* knowledge, because consciousness is inherently this opposition when it acts. 

He <note>Oedipus</note>, who had the power to solve the riddle of the Sphinx, and he <note>Orestes</note>, who trusted with childlike confidence, are both led to destruction by what the god reveals to them. The gods of the chorus are limited and restricted by the acting individuality. One aspect is the substance: the power presiding over the hearth and home and the spirit worshipped by the family, as well as the universal power dominating the state and government. Since this distinction belongs to the substance as such, when it is presented ideally, it is not individualized as two distinct forms of the substance; instead, in actual reality, it possesses the two persons of its characters. On the other hand, the distinction between knowing and not knowing falls within each actual self-consciousness; only in abstraction—within the element of universality—is it divided into two individual shapes. For the hero’s self exists only as a whole consciousness and therefore essentially includes the entire distinction belonging to the form. However, his substance is specific, and only one side of the distinguished content belongs to him. Consequently, both sides of consciousness—which have no separate individuality of their own in concrete reality—each receive their own particular form when represented ideally: one takes the form of the revealed god, and the other that of the Furies who keep themselves hidden. In part, both enjoy equal honor, while the form assumed by the substance—Zeus—is the necessity of the relationship of the two to one another. The substance is the relationship where: [1] knowledge exists for itself but finds its truth in what is simple; [2] the distinction through which actual consciousness exists is based in that inner being which destroys it; and [3] the clear, conscious assurance of certainty finds its confirmation in forgetfulness.

Once the knowledge is revealed, consciousness finds out the deceptiveness of that knowledge. Being committed, in view of the inner meaning, to one of the attributes of substance, it did violence to the other attribute and thereby gave the latter a legitimate claim against itself. While following that god who knows and reveals himself, consciousness actually seized hold of what is not revealed. It now repents for having trusted a knowledge whose ambiguous character—since this is its very nature—inevitably became apparent, along with the warnings to be found concerning it. The frenzy of the priestess, the inhuman forms of the witches, the voices of trees and birds, dreams, and so on, are not ways in which truth appears; they are warning signs of deception, of a lack of discernment, and of the individual and accidental character of knowledge. 

Or, to put it another way, the opposing power that consciousness has violated is present as explicit law and authentic right, whether as the law of the family or the law of the state. Meanwhile, consciousness pursued its own specific knowledge and hid the revealed truth from itself. The truth of these opposing powers of content and consciousness is the final result: that both are equally right, and therefore, in their opposition (which arises through action), they are equally wrong. The process of action proves their unity through the mutual destruction of both powers and the self-conscious characters. The reconciliation of this opposition with itself is the Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology.</note> of the underworld in the form of Death—or the Lethe of the upper world in the form of absolution. This is not an absolution from guilt (for consciousness cannot deny its guilt, because the act was done), but from the crime, and it provides the atoning consolation and peace of soul which absolution gives. Both are forgetfulness: the disappearance of the

The self-consciousness of the heroes must step out from behind its mask. It must be depicted as knowing itself to be the fate of both the gods of the chorus and the absolute powers themselves, and as no longer being separated from the chorus—the universal consciousness.

Comedy, then, primarily takes the form of actual self-consciousness representing itself as the Fate of the gods. These elemental beings, as universal moments, are not specific selves and are not actual. They are, indeed, given the form of individuality, but in their case, it is merely put on and does not truly suit them. The actual self does not have such an abstract moment as its substance and content. Therefore, the subject is raised above such a moment—just as it would be above a specific trait—and when wearing this mask, it expresses the irony of such a trait trying to exist on its own account. The pretentious claims of the universal abstract nature are exposed within the actual self; it is seen to be caught and held in a concrete reality, and it lets the mask fall just when it tries to be something real. The self, appearing here in its significance as something actual, plays with the mask it once put on to be its own person; but it breaks away from this appearance and pretense just as quickly, revealing its own nakedness and ordinary character. It shows that this character is not distinct from the actual self—the actor—nor from the onlooker.

## C

### REVEALED RELIGION *

Through the Religion of Art, <term>spirit</term> has passed from the form of <term>Substance</term> into that of <term>Subject</term>; for art brings out its shape and form, and imbues it with the nature of action or establishes in it the <term>self-consciousness</term> which merely disappears in the awesome substance and, in the attitude of simple trust, does not itself comprehend itself. This incarnation in human form of the <term>Divine Being</term> begins with the statue, which has in it only the outward shape of the self, while its inner life—its activity—falls outside it. In the case of the cult, however, both aspects have become one; in the outcome of the religion of art, this unity, having been completely attained, has at the same time also passed over to the extreme of the self. In this type of <term>spirit</term>, which becomes perfectly certain of itself in the individual existence of consciousness, all essential content is swallowed up and submerged. The proposition, which gives expression to this light-hearted action, runs like this: “The Self is <term>Absolute Being</term>.” The Being which was substance, and in which the self was the accidental element, has dropped to the level of a predicate; and in this <term>self-consciousness</term>, against which nothing appears in the form of objective Being, <term>spirit</term> has lost its aspect of consciousness.†

Phenomenology of Mind

This statement, “The Self is <term>Absolute Being</term>,” clearly belongs to the non-religious, concrete, and actual <term>spirit</term>; and we must recall the form that expresses it. This form will contain both the movement of that spirit and its transformation, which lowers the self to the role of a predicate and raises <term>substance</term> into <term>subject</term>. We must understand this to occur in such a way that the opposite statement does not *in itself*, or *for us*, turn substance into subject—or, what is the same thing, it does not re-establish substance so that the consciousness of spirit is pulled back to its beginning in <term>natural religion</term>. Instead, it happens in such a way that this transformation is brought about *for* and *through* <term>self-consciousness</term> itself. Since self-consciousness intentionally gives itself up, it is preserved and maintained while relinquishing itself, and it remains the subject of the substance; but because it is also *self-relinquished*, it simultaneously possesses the consciousness of this substance. In other words, since by offering itself up it produces substance as subject, this subject remains its very own self. If we then take the two propositions—where in the first, the subject merely disappears into substantiality, and in the second, the substance is merely a predicate—both sides are present in each with an opposing inequality of value. The resulting effect is that the union and merging of both natures [subject and substance] become apparent. In this union, both natures have equal value and worth; they are simultaneously essential and merely moments. Therefore, spirit is equally consciousness of itself as its objective substance, as well as a simple, self-contained self-consciousness.

<summary>This page explains how the self and substance are unified through a process of mutual relinquishment, where the self becomes a predicate and substance becomes the subject. This movement ensures that spirit is understood as both objective substance and self-contained consciousness.</summary>

# Revealed Religion

The religion of art belongs to the spirit animating the ethical sphere,* the spirit which we formerly saw sink and disappear in the condition of right—that is, in the proposition: "The self as such, the abstract person, is absolute Being." In ethical life, the self is absorbed in the spirit of its nation; it is universality filled to the full. Simple abstract individuality, however, rises out of this content, and its lightheartedness clarifies and refines it until it becomes a "person" and attains the abstract universality of right. Here, the substantial reality of the ethical spirit is lost; the abstract, insubstantial spirits of national individuals are gathered together into a pantheon. This is not a pantheon represented merely as a mental idea (*Vorstellung*), whose weak form lets each spirit alone to do as it likes, but the pantheon of abstract universality—of pure thought—which disembodies them and bestows on the spiritless self, the individual person, a complete existence on its own account.

But this self, because it is empty, has let the content go; this consciousness is Being merely within itself. Its own very existence—the legal recognition of the person—is an unfulfilled, empty abstraction. It thus really possesses only the thought of itself; in other words, as it exists there and knows itself as an object, it is something unreal. Consequently, it is merely stoic independence, the independence of thought; and this finds, by passing through the process of skepticism, its ultimate truth in that form we called the "<term>unhappy self-consciousness</term>"—the soul of despair.

The preliminary and similarly immediate form of this universality is, however, not at once the form of thought itself, of the notion as notion; it is the universality of actual reality, it is the “allness,” the collective totality of the selves, and is the elevation of existence into the sphere of representational or figurative thought (*Vorstellung*); just as in general—to take a concrete example—the “this” of sense, when transcended, is first of all the “thing” of “perception,” and is not yet the “universal” of “understanding.”

This individual human being, then, which <term>Absolute Being</term> is revealed to be, goes through in his own case as an individual the process found in sensory existence. He is the immediately present God; in consequence, His being passes over into His having been. Consciousness, for which God is thus sensuously present, ceases to see Him and to hear Him: it *has* seen Him, it *has* heard Him. And it is by the mere fact that it *has* seen and heard Him that it first becomes spiritual consciousness itself<note>Compare “He that has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14). “If I go not away the Comforter will not come unto you” (ibid. 16).</note>; or, in other words, He has now arisen in the life of Spirit, as He formerly rose before consciousness as an object existing in the sphere of sense. That is, the distinction is distinguished only from itself, and is thus the unity that has returned to itself.

There are thus three moments to be distinguished: immanent absolute Being; explicit self-existence (which is the antithesis or the express otherness of Being, and for which that Being is an object); and self-existence or self-knowledge *within* that other—within that antithetical expression. In the same way, it is a matter of indifference to coordinate a variety of other angelic shapes and forms with the simple thought of "otherness" within the Being of the Eternal, and to transfer that state of self-centeredness to them. Insofar as this condition of otherness is divided into two parts, Spirit—regarding its various moments—could be more accurately expressed numerically as a Quaternity, a four-in-one; or (because the multiplicity splits again into two parts, namely one part which has remained good and the other which has become evil), it might be expressed as a Quinity.

However, counting these moments can be regarded as completely useless. For one thing, what is being distinguished is itself just as truly single and one—namely, the thought of distinction, which is only one thought—just as the thought is the very element being distinguished (the second as opposed to the first). For another thing, counting is useless because the thought that grasps the "many in one" must be broken down from its universality and must be distinguished into more than just three or four separate components. The alienation of the Divine Nature is thus established in its two-sided form: the self of Spirit and its simple thought are the two moments whose absolute unity is Spirit itself. Its alienation from itself consists in these two falling away from each other, where one has an unequal value compared to the other. This disparity is, therefore, twofold in character, and two connections arise that share the moments just mentioned. In one, the Divine Being represents what is essential, while natural existence and the self are non-essential and are to be discarded. In the other, on the contrary, self-existence is considered essential, while the Divine, pure and simple, is considered non-essential. Their mediating but empty foundation is existence in general—the mere commonality of these two moments.

The resolution of this opposition does not happen through a struggle between the two elements when they are represented as separate and independent beings. Because of their independence, each must inherently, through its own concept, dissolve itself from within. The struggle occurs first in the area where both cease to be this mixture of thought and independent existence and instead confront each other merely as thoughts. For in that case, being specific concepts, they essentially exist only in a relationship of opposition; *as* independent entities, on the other hand, they have their essential nature outside of that opposition. Their movement is thus free, self-determined, and unique to themselves. Only these two propositions together make the whole complete; and when the first is asserted and maintained, it must be met and opposed by insisting on the other with unwavering persistence. ### VIII

## ABSOLUTE KNOWLEDGE*

<note>See above, p. 684. "Absolute Knowledge" is at once the completion of experience and, on the historical side, constructive philosophy: see below, p. 815 ff.</note>

**THE** Spirit manifested in revealed religion has not as yet overcome its perspective of consciousness as such; or, what is the same thing, its concrete self-consciousness is not at this stage the object it is aware of. Spirit as a whole and the distinct moments within it fall within the sphere of representational thinking; they are mental representations with the form of objective reality. The content of this representational thought is Absolute Spirit. All that remains to be done now is to cancel and transcend this mere form; or rather, because the form belongs to consciousness as such, its true meaning must have already emerged in the shapes and modes that consciousness has previously assumed.

The overcoming of the object of consciousness in this way is not to be understood one-sidedly as meaning that the object shows itself returning into the self. It has a more definite and specific meaning: it means that the object as such presents itself to the self as a vanishing factor; and, furthermore, that the emptying—the surrender—of self-consciousness itself establishes thinghood, and that this setting aside of self-consciousness

<summary>This page marks the transition to Absolute Knowledge, explaining that Spirit in revealed religion still views its content through mental representations rather than fully realized self-consciousness. It establishes that the final step is to transcend the objective form of these representations, where the surrender of self-consciousness actually constitutes the reality of the object.</summary>
<keywords>Spirit, revealed religion, consciousness, self-consciousness, Absolute Spirit, Absolute Knowledge, thinghood, representational thinking, objectivity</keywords>

has not merely a negative, but a positive significance—a significance not merely for us or *per se*, but for self-consciousness itself. The negative aspect of the object, where it cancels its own existence, acquires a positive significance for self-consciousness; or, to put it another way, self-consciousness knows this nothingness of the object because, on the one hand, self-consciousness relinquishes itself. In doing so, it establishes itself as an object or, because of the indivisible unity characterizing its self-existence, sets up the object as itself. On the other hand, there is also this other moment in the process: self-consciousness has just as truly cancelled and done away with this self-relinquishment and objectification and has resumed them into itself; it is thus at home with itself in its otherness. This is the movement of consciousness, and in this process, consciousness is the totality of its moments.

Consciousness, at the same time, had to establish a relation to the object in all its aspects and phases, and grasp its meaning from the point of view of each of them. This totality of its determinate characteristics makes the object *per se* and inherently a spiritual reality; and it becomes so in truth for consciousness when the latter apprehends every individual one of them as self—that is, when it adopts toward them the spiritual relationship just described.

The object is, then, partly immediate existence, a *thing* in general—corresponding to immediate consciousness; partly an alteration of itself, its relatedness (or existence-for-another and existence-for-self), and its *determinateness*—corresponding to perception; and partly essential being or in the form of a *universal*—corresponding to intelligence or understanding. The object as a whole is

These three specific aspects, then, determine the ways in which consciousness must come to know the object in the form of self. This knowledge of which we are speaking is, however, not knowledge in the sense of pure conceptual comprehension of the object; here, this knowledge is to be taken as a developing process. It has to be taken in its various moments and set forth in the manner appropriate to consciousness as such; and the moments of the notion proper—of pure and absolute knowledge—are to assume the form of modes or attitudes of consciousness. For that reason, the object does not yet appear as the inner essence of Spirit, in the way this has just been expressed, when it is present in consciousness as such. The procedure consciousness adopts regarding the object is not that of considering it either in this totality as such or in the pure conceptual form; it is partly that of a mode or attitude of consciousness in general, and partly a multitude of such modes which *we* <note>who analyze the process</note> gather together, and in which the totality of the moments of the object and of the procedure of consciousness can be shown merely resolved into their separate elements.

To understand this method of grasping the object, where apprehension is a form or mode of consciousness, we have here only to recall the previous forms of consciousness which appeared before us earlier in the argument.

That judgment, then—"the ego is a thing"—at first glance has no spiritual content, or rather, it is the very absence of spirituality. Things are simply and solely useful and profitable, and are only to be considered from the perspective of their utility.

But knowledge of the thing is not yet finished at this point. The thing must become known as the self, not merely in regard to the immediacy of its being and its specific determinateness, but also in the sense of essence or inner reality. This mode of experience thinks of its knowledge as the absolute essential element, and knows no other objective being than pure will or pure knowledge. It is nothing but merely this will and this knowledge. Anything else possesses merely non-essential being—that is, being that has no inherent nature *per se*, but is only an empty husk. Insofar as the moral consciousness, in its view of the world, lets existence drop out of the self, it just as truly reclaims and takes this existence back again into the self. In the form of conscience, finally, it is no longer this incessant alternation between the “placing” and the “displacing” (or dissembling) of existence and the self; it knows that its existence as such is this pure certainty of its own self. The objective element, into which *qua* acting it puts itself forth, is nothing else than pure knowledge of itself by itself.

These are the moments which compose the reconciliation of spirit with its own consciousness proper.
