As we have considered them, they fall apart at the beginning. In the order in which the modes or types of consciousness appeared before us, consciousness reached the individual moments of that order, as well as their unification, long before religion ever gave its object the shape and mold of actual self-consciousness. The unification of both aspects has not yet been revealed; it is this that concludes this series of embodiments of spiritual life. In this unification, spirit reaches the point where it knows itself not only as it is inherently in itself, or in terms of its absolute content, nor only as it is objectively for itself in terms of its bare form devoid of content, or in terms of self-consciousness, but as it is in its self-completeness—as it is inherently and explicitly, in itself and for itself.

This unification has, however, already taken place implicitly; it has done so in religion, in the return of the objective representation (*Vorstellung* <note>A German term meaning a mental representation or figurative thought.</note>) into self-consciousness, but not according to the proper form. This is because the religious aspect is the aspect of the essentially independent (*Ansich* <note>A technical term meaning "in-itself" or the inherent essence.</note>) and stands in contrast to the process of self-consciousness. The unification, therefore, belongs to this other aspect, which by contrast is the aspect of reflection into the self. It is that side which contains both itself and its opposite, and contains them not only implicitly (*an sich*) or in a general way, but explicitly (*für sich*) or as expressly developed and distinguished. The content, as well as the other aspect of self-conscious spirit (insofar as it is the other aspect), have been revealed and are here in their completeness: the unification still lacking is the simple unity of the <term>notion</term>. This <term>notion</term> is also already provided within the aspect of self-consciousness; but as it previously appeared before us

That is to say, the "beautiful soul" is its own knowledge of itself in its pure transparent unity; self-consciousness, which knows this pure knowledge of pure inwardness to be spirit, is not merely an intuition of the divine, but is the self-intuition of God Himself.

Since this notion remains fixedly opposed to its realization, it is the one-sided form which we previously saw vanish into thin air, yet also take on a positive external embodiment and advance further. Through the process of realization, this self-consciousness—which lacks objective content—stops clinging only to itself; the abstract determinateness of the notion, as opposed to its fulfillment, is canceled and superseded. Its self-consciousness attains the form of universality; and what remains is its true notion, the notion that has attained its realization—the notion in its truth, which is to say, in unity with its externalization. It is knowledge of pure knowledge, not in the sense of an abstract essence such as duty is, but in the sense of an essential being which is *this* particular knowledge, this individual pure self-consciousness which is at the same time an *object*; for the object is the self-existing self.

This notion obtained its fulfillment partly from the acts performed by the spirit that is sure of itself, and partly from religion. In religion, it obtained the absolute content *qua* content, or in the form of a mental representation or of "otherness" for consciousness. By this process of action, <term>spirit</term> has come to light in the form of pure universality of knowledge, which is self-consciousness as self-consciousness—the simple unity of knowledge. Now, in actual reality, the knowing substance is reached earlier than its form—earlier than the form of the <term>notion</term>. For the substance is the undeveloped inherent nature, the fundamental <term>notion</term> in its inert simplicity, the state of inwardness or the self of <term>spirit</term> that has not yet been objectified. What is present, what does exist, is in the shape of unexpressed simplicity, the undeveloped immediate, or the object of representational consciousness in general. Because knowledge (*Erkennen*) is a spiritual state of consciousness—which is only aware of what is implicit and inherent insofar as this is a being for the self and a being of the self or a <term>notion</term>—knowledge initially has a meager object. In contrast, the substance and the consciousness of this substance are richer in content. 

In such a case, revelation is, in fact, concealment; for the substance here is still an existence without a self, and nothing but the certainty of self is manifest or revealed to it. To begin with, therefore, only abstract moments fall to self-consciousness when it deals with the substance. But since these moments are pure activities and must move forward by their very nature, self-consciousness enriches itself until it has torn the entire substance from consciousness and absorbed the whole structure of the substance, with all its constituent elements, into itself. Since this negative attitude toward objectivity is also positive—establishing and fixing the content—it continues until it has produced these elements out of itself and thereby reinstated them once more as objects of consciousness. ...the whole comes into being. In consciousness, on the other hand, the whole—though not as conceptually understood—precedes the individual moments.

Time is simply the <term>notion</term> existing in a definite way, presented to consciousness in the form of empty, pure intuition. Therefore, <term>spirit</term> necessarily appears in time, and it appears in time as long as it does not grasp its pure <term>notion</term>—that is, as long as it does not annul time. Time is the pure self in external form, perceived through intuition but not yet grasped and understood by the self; it is the <term>notion</term> directly perceived through intuition. When this <term>notion</term> grasps itself, it overcomes its temporal character, conceptually understands intuition, and becomes intuition that is both understood and understanding through concepts. Time, therefore, appears as the destiny and necessity of <term>spirit</term> when <term>spirit</term> is not yet complete within itself. It is the necessity that compels <term>spirit</term> to increase and enrich the share that self-consciousness has in consciousness; to set in motion the immediacy of its inherent nature (which is the form in which the <term>substance</term> is present in consciousness); or, conversely, to realize and make manifest what is inherent—viewed as inward and immanent—and to make manifest what is at first internal; that is, to justify and secure for it the certainty of self.

For this reason, it must be said that nothing is consciously known that does not fall within experience, or (as it is also expressed) which is not *felt* to be true, which is not given as an inwardly revealed eternal truth, as a sacred object of belief, or whatever other expressions we choose to employ. For experience consists exactly in this: that the content—and the content is <term>spirit</term>—is, in its inherent nature, <term>substance</term> and therefore an object.

<summary>This page explains that spirit must exist in time until it achieves conceptual self-understanding, at which point it transcends temporal constraints. This development occurs through experience, where the internal substance of spirit is made manifest and certain to self-consciousness.</summary>

<keywords>Absolute Knowledge, consciousness, notion, intuition, spirit, time, self-consciousness, substance, experience</keywords>

of consciousness. But this <term>substance</term>, which constitutes <term>spirit</term>, is the development of itself explicitly into what it is inherently and implicitly; and only through this process of reflecting itself into itself is it then essentially and truly <term>spirit</term>. It is inherently the movement that constitutes the process of knowledge—the transformation of that implicit inherent nature into explicitness and objectivity, of <term>substance</term> into <term>subject</term>, of the object of consciousness into the object of self-consciousness—that is, into an object that is simultaneously superseded and transcended—in other words, into the <term>notion</term>. This transforming process is a cycle that returns into itself, a cycle that presupposes its beginning and reaches its beginning only at the end. Since <term>spirit</term>, then, is necessarily this process of self-distinction, it appears as a single whole, intuitively perceived, standing against its simple <term>self-consciousness</term>. And because that whole is the aspect being distinguished, it is divided into the intuitively perceived pure <term>notion</term>, Time, and the content, which is the inherent implicit nature. <term>Substance</term>, as <term>subject</term>, involves the necessity—at first an *inner* necessity—to set forth within itself what it inherently is, to show itself to be <term>spirit</term>. The completed systematic expression in objective form then becomes, at the same time, the reflection of <term>substance</term>, the development of it into a self or <term>subject</term>. Consequently, until and unless <term>spirit</term> is inherently completed, completed as a <term>world-spirit</term>, it cannot reach its completion as <term>self-conscious spirit</term>. The content of religion, therefore, expresses what <term>spirit</term> is earlier in time than <term>speculative science</term> does; but science alone is the perfect form in which <term>spirit</term> truly knows itself.

<header>Absolute Knowledge</header>

Knowledge of itself constitutes the task which <term>spirit</term> accomplishes in the concrete, actual shape of <term>History</term>. The <term>religious communion</term>, insofar as it is at the outset the substance of <term>Absolute Spirit</term>, is the crude form of consciousness. This consciousness has an existence that is all the harsher and more barbaric the deeper its inner spirit is; and its inarticulate, stolid self has all the harder task in dealing with its essence—the unconceived content that is alien to its consciousness. Only when it has surrendered the hope of canceling that foreignness by an external (that is, alien) method does it turn to itself, to its own peculiar world in the actual present. It turns there because to supersede that alien method means returning into <term>self-consciousness</term>. It thus discovers this world in the living present to be its own property; and so it has taken the first step to descend from the ideal <term>intelligible world</term> (the world of the <term>intellect</term>), or rather to endow the abstract element of the intellect with concrete selfhood.

Through “<term>observation</term>,” on the one hand, it finds existence in the shape of thought and comprehends existence; and, conversely, it finds existence in its thought.* When, in the first instance, it has expressed the immediate unity of thought and existence—of abstract Being and Self—in this abstract way; and when it has expressed the primal principle of “Light” in a purer form, namely as a unity of extension and existence (for “existence” is an ultimate simple term more akin to thought than “Light”), and in this way has revived again in thought the <term>Substance of the Orient</term>,† the <term>Absolute Substance</term> of <term>Eastern Religions</term>; thereupon <term>spirit</term> at once recoils in horror from this abstract unity, from this

selfless substance, and maintains against it the principle of subjective Individuality.* But after spirit has relinquished this principle and brought it through the ordeal of culture, has thereby made it an objective existence and established it throughout the whole of existence, has arrived at the idea of "Utility" † and in the sphere of absolute freedom has found the key to existence to be the Individual Will,‡—after these stages, spirit then brings to light the thought that lies in its inmost depths, and expresses ultimate Reality in the form Ego = Ego.§

This "Ego identical with Ego" is, however, an inward, self-reflecting process; for since this identity as absolute negativity is absolute distinction, the self-identity of the Ego stands in contrast to this absolute distinction, which—being pure distinction and at the same time objective to the self that knows itself—must be expressed as Time. In this way, just as ultimate Reality was formerly expressed as the unity of thought and extension, it would here be interpreted as the unity of thought and time. But distinction left to itself, unresting, unhalting time, actually collapses upon itself; it is the objective stillness, the stable continuity of extension; while this latter is pure identity with self—it is the Ego.

Again, the Ego is not merely the self, it is the identity of the self with itself. This identity, however, is a complete and immediate unity with the self; in other words, this Subject is just as much Substance. It would not be conceived as Spirit, which reflects on itself and reflects itself back into itself. Knowledge would appear to have come upon things—realities distinct from knowledge itself—and to have arrived at the distinctions between an endless variety of things without anyone understanding how or where all of this originated.

Spirit, however, has shown itself to be neither the mere withdrawal of self-consciousness into its own pure inwardness nor the mere absorption of self-consciousness into a blank Substance lacking all distinctions. Spirit is the movement of the self which empties itself and immerses itself within its own substance; as a subject (*qua* subject), it both emerges from that substance into itself—making its substance an object and a content—and also overcomes this distinction between objectivity and content. That first reflection out of immediacy is the subject’s distinction of itself from its substance; it is the concept in a state of <term>self-diremption</term>, the process of the self becoming a subject, and the emergence of the pure ego into being. The <term>notion</term> is the necessity for and the emergence of <term>existence</term>; it has <term>substance</term> as its essential nature and is <term>self-subsistent</term>. But this <term>self-subsistent</term> <term>existence</term> is the <term>notion</term> established and realized in a determinate form; it is thereby the <term>notion's</term> own inherent movement—that of descending into the bare and simple <term>substance</term>, which only becomes a subject by being this <term>negativity</term> and going through this process.

The **Ego** does not have to take its stand on the form of <term>self-consciousness</term> in opposition to the form of <term>substantiality</term> and <term>objectivity</term>, as if it were afraid of emptying itself and becoming objective. The power of <term>spirit</term> lies rather in remaining one with itself even when giving itself up; because it is self-contained and <term>self-subsistent</term>, it establishes both its explicit self-existence and its implicit inherent nature as mere moments. Nor, again, is the **Ego** a *<term>tertium quid</term>* which casts distinctions back into the abyss of the <term>Absolute</term> and declares them all to mean the same thing there. On the contrary, true knowledge lies rather in the seeming inactivity which merely watches and considers how the distinct element proceeds—how it is self-moved by its very nature and returns again into its own unity.

With <term>absolute knowledge</term>, then, **Spirit** has concluded the process of its various forms and modes, insofar as—in assuming these various shapes and forms—it is affected by the insurmountable distinction which consciousness implies <note>that is, the distinction of consciousness from its object or content</note>. **Spirit** has attained the pure element of its existence: the <term>notion</term>. Given the freedom of its own existence, the content is the self that empties and surrenders itself to <term>objectivity</term>; in other words, that

Content is the immediate unity of self-knowledge. The pure process of surrendering itself to externality constitutes—when we consider this process in its relation to the content—the necessity of this content. The diversity of content, *as* something specific and defined, is due to relationship and is not inherent; it is the restless activity of canceling and moving beyond itself, or its negativity. Thus, this necessity or diversity, like its free existence, is also the self; and in this form of the self, where existence is immediately thought, the content is a <term>notion</term>. 

Seeing, then, that Spirit has attained the <term>notion</term>, it unfolds its existence and develops its processes in this atmosphere of its life and is *Systematic Science*. The moments of its process are no longer presented in Science as definite modes or forms of consciousness. Instead—since the distinction that consciousness implies has returned to the self and become a distinction within the self—they are presented as definite <term>notions</term>, and as the organic, self-explaining, and self-constituted process of these concepts. 

While in the *Phenomenology of Mind* each moment is the distinction between knowledge and truth, and the process in which that distinction is canceled and transcended, *Systematic Science* does not contain this distinction or the overcoming of it. Rather, since each moment has the form of the <term>notion</term>, it unites the objective form of truth and the knowing self in an immediate unity. In Science, the individual moment does not appear as the process of passing back and forth from consciousness or representation to self-consciousness and vice versa; there, the pure form is liberated from the condition of being a mere appearance in consciousness. Nature is Spirit stripped of self and surrendered to the external world. The other aspect in which Spirit comes into being, however, is *History*. This is a process defined by knowledge—a conscious, self-mediating process where Spirit is surrendered to and emptied into Time. But this form of abandonment is also a self-emptying; the negative is negative of itself. This path of becoming presents a slow procession and succession of spiritual shapes and forms—a gallery of images. Each image is endowed with the entire wealth of Spirit, and they move so slowly simply because the self must permeate and absorb all the richness of its substance. Since its achievement consists of Spirit knowing what it is and fully comprehending its substance, this knowledge results in Spirit becoming a subject—a state in which Spirit leaves its external existence behind and commits itself to the attitude of Recollection (*Erinnerung*). In this inward turn, Spirit is engulfed in the darkness and night of its own self-consciousness; however, its vanished existence is preserved there.
